In this study, we present TipsC, a novel approach aimed at enhancing programming Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) by providing learners with real-time tips and corrections during coding exercises. The primary objective of this work is to address the common challenges faced by learners in programming MOOCs, such as syntactic errors, logical mistakes, and inefficient coding practices. Through TipsC, we aim to improve the overall learning experience and outcomes for participants in programming courses.  The results of our research demonstrate the effectiveness of TipsC in significantly reducing the time taken to correct errors and complete coding tasks. By incorporating adaptive feedback mechanisms based on common errors identified in learners' submissions, TipsC offers personalized guidance to help individuals overcome specific programming hurdles. This tailored approach not only accelerates the learning process but also enhances retention and comprehension of coding concepts.  Key ideas behind TipsC involve leveraging machine learning algorithms to analyze learner code submissions, identify errors, and deliver targeted feedback in real-time. Our methodology includes the development of a robust feedback generation system that integrates seamlessly with existing MOOC platforms to offer immediate assistance to learners as they work through coding assignments. Overall, TipsC represents a pioneering solution to enhance the effectiveness of programming MOOCs by providing valuable tips and corrections tailored to individual learner needs.

We investigate the origin of non-Maxwellian electron velocity distribution functions (VDFs) in the solar wind and propose a connection to nanoflare activity in the solar corona. Traditional models assume a Maxwellian distribution of particle velocities; however, recent observations have increasingly identified deviations, particularly in the high-energy tails of electron VDFs. This study aims to elucidate the processes contributing to this non-Maxwellian behavior by exploring the role of nanoflares, which are hypothesized to impart energy through impulsive heating events. We employ a combination of observational data from spacecraft missions and advanced numerical simulations that account for coronal heating and electron transport mechanisms. Our findings reveal that nanoflares significantly enhance the high-energy tails of electron VDFs in the corona, which subsequently propagates into the heliosphere, manifesting as non-Maxwellian distributions in the solar wind. By modeling the energy deposition and redistribution associated with nanoflare-driven turbulence, we demonstrate that these small-scale energetic events can satisfactorily account for the observed discrepancies from Maxwellian behavior. Furthermore, we identify specific parameter regimes under which nanoflares robustly influence electron dynamics, offering predictive insights into solar wind electron characteristics. This research provides compelling evidence linking coronal heating mechanisms to solar wind properties and enhances our understanding of heliophysical processes. By elucidating the connection between nanoflares and electron VDFs, this study contributes to the broader comprehension of solar-terrestrial interactions and underscores the importance of incorporating non-Maxwellian considerations in solar wind models.

The present study investigates the influence of cobalt content on the electrochemical performance and structural stability of nickel-cobalt-aluminum oxide (NCA) cathode materials, a promising candidate for advanced lithium-ion batteries. As enhancements in energy density and cycle life are imperative for next-generation battery applications, optimizing the composition of NCA materials is of critical importance. Our research focuses on varying cobalt concentrations within the cathode material and examining its effects on key electrochemical properties, including capacity retention, rate capability, and cyclic performance. Utilizing a combination of X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), the structural stability and morphological changes of the NCA cathodes were systematically analyzed. Electrochemical assessments were conducted using galvanostatic charge-discharge tests, cyclic voltammetry, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. Our findings indicate that an optimal range of cobalt content significantly enhances capacity retention and rate capability while mitigating structural degradation over extended cycling. Specifically, cobalt aids in stabilizing the layered structure by reducing phase transitions that typically hinder lithium-ion diffusion. However, excessive cobalt concentrations were found to diminish electrochemical performance due to higher polarization and impedance. In conclusion, the study elucidates a critical balance of cobalt content essential for optimizing the performance and longevity of NCA cathodes, providing valuable insights for the design of high-performance lithium-ion batteries. Future research should explore the synergistic effects of cobalt with other dopants to further augment the capabilities of NCA materials.

Nuclear alpha-particle condensates represent a novel phenomenon in the study of nuclear physics, primarily due to their implications for understanding the nature of interactions within dense nuclear matter. This research aims to explore the formation, properties, and implications of alpha-particle condensates in heavy nuclei, particularly in the context of nuclear structure and stability. Using advanced computational models and quantum statistical approaches, we investigate the conditions under which these condensates emerge and their correlations with nucleon configurations. Key findings indicate that alpha-particle condensates exhibit significant collective behaviors that influence the binding energy and decay modes of heavy nuclei. Furthermore, these condensates are shown to play an essential role in the synthesis of elements through nucleosynthesis processes in stars, thereby linking theoretical concepts to astrophysical observations. Additionally, the research highlights potential applications in nuclear reactors and the development of novel materials in nuclear science. In conclusion, understanding nuclear alpha-particle condensates not only enriches the theoretical framework of nuclear interactions but also opens new avenues for both fundamental and applied research in physics, with broader implications for cosmology and material science.

This study investigates the properties and structural characteristics of essentially 4-edge-connected cubic bricks, which are a prominent topic in the realm of discrete geometry and computational topology. The primary objective is to analyze the conditions under which cubic bricks maintain 4-edge connectivity while exploring their implications for graph theory and structure stability. Employing a combination of combinatorial and computational methods, we systematically examine the various configurations of cubic bricks, focusing on the relationships between vertex arrangements and edge connectivity. Additionally, we introduce a novel algorithm designed to efficiently identify and construct essentially 4-edge-connected cubic bricks within larger frameworks.   Key findings reveal that certain configurations enhance the robustness of edge connectivity, facilitating a deeper understanding of the underlying principles governing these geometric structures. Our results also indicate that the presence of specific vertex distributions significantly influences the stability of the cubic bricks. The study concludes that the characterization of essentially 4-edge-connected cubic bricks not only contributes to the theoretical foundations of graph theory but also has practical implications in fields such as materials science and architectural engineering, where stability and connectivity are paramount. This research lays the groundwork for future explorations into advanced geometric configurations and their applications in various technological domains.

Our research focuses on the efficient matching of expert consultants in the e-healthcare sector using a two-sided matching approach. The problem we aim to solve is the complexity and time-consuming nature of the current consultant hiring process in e-healthcare organizations. By adopting a two-sided matching framework, we seek to optimize the allocation of consultants to projects based on their expertise and the specific requirements of each project.   Through simulations and case studies, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach in improving the overall efficiency of the consultant hiring process. The results indicate that our method can significantly reduce the time and resources spent on matching consultants to projects while ensuring a better fit between the consultants' skills and the project requirements.   Our key idea revolves around creating a structured matching system that takes into account the preferences of both the consultants and the e-healthcare organizations, leading to mutually beneficial outcomes for both parties. The methodology involves developing a mathematical model based on preferences and constraints provided by the consultants and organizations, followed by an algorithm to facilitate the matching process.  In conclusion, our study contributes to the optimization of consultant allocation in the e-healthcare industry by introducing a two-sided matching approach that enhances the overall efficiency of the hiring process.

We present our findings from a comprehensive survey of hydrides in low- to high-mass young stellar objects (YSOs), which reveals critical constraints on the ultraviolet (UV) and X-ray irradiation environments characteristic of these stellar systems. Our primary objective was to elucidate the impact of high-energy radiation on the chemical and physical properties of hydrides, particularly focusing on molecules such as H₂O, CH₄, and NH₃. Utilizing high-resolution infrared spectroscopy, we systematically measured hydride abundances in various YSOs, correlating these data with the proximity to massive stellar sources and their respective emission characteristics.  Through our analysis, we identified distinct patterns that correlate increased radiation fields with a depletion of certain hydrides, suggesting that intense UV and X-ray irradiation plays a significant role in the dissociation processes affecting these molecular species. Moreover, we employed computational models to simulate the effects of varying radiation intensities, demonstrating that environments enriched in high-energy emissions produce markedly different hydride profiles compared to those exposed to lower radiation levels. Our results indicate that the chemical evolution of hydrides in YSOs is inherently linked to the stellar radiation environment and can serve as an important indicator of the formative processes at play in stellar nurseries.  Ultimately, our work contributes to a deeper understanding of the interactions between radiation and molecular abundance in the early stages of star formation, paving the way for future investigations into the feedback mechanisms between stellar activity and molecular evolution in astrophysical context.

Gravitational-wave astronomy has provided unprecedented insights into cosmic events, yet the detection and characterization of unmodelled gravitational-wave transients remain a significant challenge. This study applies Bayesian inference to the analysis of unmodelled gravitational-wave transients, aiming to improve their detection and understanding. The approach leverages the flexibility of Bayesian statistics to make probabilistic inferences about poorly characterized signals, offering an advantage over traditional methods constrained by model assumptions. We develop a robust framework integrating Bayesian inference algorithms with data from gravitational-wave observatories, facilitating a comprehensive search for transients without reliance on predefined signal models. The methodology incorporates prior distributions to accommodate the uncertain nature of transient features and employs Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling to explore the parameter space efficiently. Our key findings demonstrate that this Bayesian approach not only enhances the sensitivity of transient detection but also enables reliable characterization of their astrophysical parameters, often revealing features overlooked by model-dependent techniques. This increase in sensitivity could provide vital clues about the population and nature of elusive transient sources, such as core-collapse supernovae or neutron star mergers with unconventional dynamics. Conclusively, the research underscores the effectiveness of Bayesian inference as a powerful tool in gravitational-wave data analysis, presenting a pathway to detect and study unmodeled transients with high accuracy. This advancement promises to broaden the horizon of gravitational-wave astronomy and enhance our understanding of complex astrophysical phenomena.

The abstract for the research paper focusing on "Wall-bounded flow over a realistically rough superhydrophobic surface" is as follows  This study investigates the flow dynamics over a surface characterized by both microscale and macroscale roughness, which exhibits superhydrophobic properties. The primary objective was to understand how the combination of hydrophobicity and roughness affects wall-bounded fluid flow characteristics. Utilizing computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations alongside experimental measurements, the research aimed to elucidate the interaction between the surface morphology and the flow behavior.  The methodology involved fabricating a realistic rough superhydrophobic surface and conducting detailed CFD simulations using established turbulence models. Experiments were conducted to validate the simulation results, employing high-speed imaging techniques to capture flow patterns directly at the surface. Key findings revealed that the superhydrophobic nature of the surface significantly altered the flow regime, leading to reduced frictional drag and enhanced heat transfer rates compared to smooth surfaces. Additionally, the roughness introduced complex flow structures, including vortices and recirculation zones, which influenced the overall flow stability and boundary layer thickness.  In conclusion, the research demonstrates that the integration of superhydrophobicity with realistic roughness can markedly influence wall-bounded flows, offering potential applications in enhancing thermal management systems and reducing fluid resistance in engineering applications. Further investigation into the underlying mechanisms will be necessary to optimize these effects for practical use.

This study explores the development and application of multi-function convolutional neural networks (MFCNNs) aimed at enhancing image classification performance. Our approach integrates multiple functions within a single CNN architecture to address diverse aspects of image data, thereby optimizing overall classification accuracy. Initially, we faced challenges in effectively managing the complexity and interdependencies among various tasks. To overcome these issues, we employed a modular design where each function is responsible for specific features such as color, texture, and object recognition. We also utilized transfer learning and data augmentation techniques to improve model robustness and generalization capabilities. Through extensive experimentation on benchmark datasets, we achieved significant improvements in classification accuracy across multiple tasks. The key methodologies involved iterative refinement of network architectures, hyperparameter tuning, and rigorous validation through cross-validation. The results demonstrate that MFCNNs can significantly outperform traditional single-task CNNs by leveraging synergies between different image analysis tasks, leading to more versatile and efficient image classification systems.

In this study, we investigate the problem of determining the endpoint of a path within a d-dimensional grid and extend our analysis to other graph structures. We present a novel algorithm that efficiently identifies the terminal node of a given path within the d-dimensional grid. The algorithm employs a breadth-first search strategy tailored to exploit the inherent symmetry and regularity of the grid structure, significantly reducing computational complexity compared to general graph traversal methods.  Our initial approach involved implementing standard BFS algorithms but faced inefficiencies due to redundant computations across different dimensions. To address these issues, we introduced a dimension-specific traversal strategy that skips unnecessary computations, thereby optimizing performance. Extensive simulations were conducted on various grid sizes and dimensions, demonstrating the efficacy of our method in terms of both time and space efficiency.  The results indicate that our algorithm outperforms existing approaches by up to 30% in execution time, especially for large grids. Furthermore, we extended our findings to other graph types such as complete graphs and random graphs, showing that our method can be generalized with minor adjustments. This versatility makes it a robust solution applicable beyond just the d-dimensional grid, making it valuable for applications requiring efficient path termination detection in diverse network configurations.

This study explores the impact of epistasis on fitness landscapes and its implications for evolutionary dynamics under various constraints. We employed a combination of theoretical models and computational simulations to investigate how genetic interactions affect the ruggedness and complexity of fitness landscapes. Our findings indicate that strong epistatic interactions lead to more complex landscapes, where small changes can have disproportionately large effects on fitness. We also observed that such landscapes are particularly challenging for populations to navigate, leading to higher rates of extinction. To address these challenges, we developed a new method to quantify epistatic effects using genetic distances between mutations. This approach allows us to identify regions within the genome that contribute most significantly to the landscape's ruggedness. Our results highlight the importance of considering epistasis in the design of experimental evolution studies and in predicting evolutionary outcomes under different environmental conditions.

This research paper introduces a robust mobile object tracking approach based on multiple feature similarity and trajectory filtering. The objective of this study is to enhance the accuracy and robustness of object tracking in mobile applications. The methodology involves the integration of multiple feature similarity measures, such as color, texture, and shape, to improve tracking performance under various conditions. Additionally, trajectory filtering techniques are employed to refine the tracking results and reduce errors caused by occlusions or noisy data.   Key findings from this research reveal that the proposed method significantly improves tracking accuracy compared to traditional single-feature-based approaches. By combining multiple feature similarities and applying trajectory filtering, the tracking system demonstrates better adaptability to complex scenarios, such as object appearance changes and occlusions. Experimental results on benchmark datasets show that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in terms of tracking precision and robustness.  In conclusion, the novel combination of multiple feature similarity and trajectory filtering techniques offers a promising solution for enhancing the robustness of mobile object tracking systems. This research contributes to advancing the field of computer vision and provides a practical framework for improving object tracking performance in real-world applications.

The massless spin-boson model is a critical area of investigation due to its implications on understanding the interaction between quantum fields and spin systems. This research addresses the velocity estimates and soft mode bounds within the model, providing insight into the behavior of bosonic particles in interaction with spins under minimal velocity conditions. The objective of the study is to establish a comprehensive framework to derive effective bounds on both the velocity of the evolution of the system and the dynamics of soft modes, which represent low-energy fluctuations. The methodology involves using advanced spectral analysis techniques and perturbative methods to analyze the Hamiltonian governing the system, specifically examining the impact of the massless nature of bosons on system stability and equilibrium. Key findings reveal that, despite the absence of intrinsic mass, there exists a finite minimal velocity threshold beyond which certain dynamical properties are maintained, thereby ensuring system stability under specific conditions. Furthermore, soft mode contributions are shown to have a limited impact on system equilibrium at velocities exceeding this threshold due to intrinsic compensatory mechanisms. In conclusion, the results provide crucial insights into the stabilizing factors within massless spin-boson systems, highlighting the interplay between minimal velocity constraints and soft mode dynamics. These findings are anticipated to have significant implications in quantum field theory and the development of quantum technologies, offering a deeper understanding of low-energy phenomena in bosonic fields and their potential harness in future quantum applications.

The study examines the evolution of galaxy luminosity and stellar-mass functions from redshift $z=1$ using the Dark Energy Survey (DES) Science Verification data. The primary objective was to investigate how these properties have changed over cosmic time, providing insights into the assembly history and star formation histories of galaxies.  To achieve this, a comprehensive analysis was conducted, employing photometric redshifts and stellar masses estimated from the multi-band imaging data. The sample selection focused on galaxies brighter than $i=24.5$, ensuring a representative sample for the analysis. A Bayesian framework was utilized to model the luminosity and stellar mass functions, accounting for uncertainties in the photometric redshifts and stellar mass estimates.  Key findings revealed that both the luminosity and stellar mass functions show significant changes with redshift, with galaxies becoming more luminous and massive at higher redshifts. This trend suggests an increase in star formation activity and the growth of massive galaxies during the early universe. Additionally, there was a noticeable decline in the number density of low-mass galaxies at $z \approx 1$, indicating that smaller galaxies were either quenched or lost their star-forming capabilities by this epoch.  The results highlight the importance of understanding the evolution of galaxies and their stellar populations as they trace back to the epoch of reionization. These findings contribute to our broader understanding of galaxy formation and evolution and provide valuable constraints for cosmological models involving dark energy.

The abstract for the research paper titled "Fast Simulation of Gaussian-Mode Scattering for Precision Interferometry" outlines the objectives, methodologies, and key findings related to the simulation of Gaussian-mode scattering for enhancing precision in interferometric measurements.  This study focuses on developing efficient computational tools to simulate the scattering patterns of Gaussian modes within interferometers, which are crucial for achieving high precision in optical measurements. These algorithms are optimized for performance, ensuring that they can handle complex scenarios with minimal computational resources. The simulations are validated against existing analytical models and experimental data to ensure reliability.  Key findings indicate significant improvements in the computational efficiency of simulating Gaussian-mode scattering, reducing processing times by up to 80% compared to traditional methods. This enhancement allows for more frequent recalibrations and adjustments of interferometric systems, leading to improved measurement accuracy.  In conclusion, this research successfully accelerates the simulation process of Gaussian-mode scattering, paving the way for enhanced precision in interferometry applications. The developed techniques offer substantial benefits for both theoretical investigations and practical implementations in fields such as gravitational wave detection and astronomical observations.

In this work, we explore the problem of computing all maps into a sphere. The primary aim is to develop a methodology for efficiently determining the set of all possible mappings from various surfaces to a sphere. Our results showcase a novel algorithm that systematically generates and analyzes these maps, offering a comprehensive understanding of their characteristics and properties. By leveraging advanced computational techniques, we are able to handle complex surfaces and provide insights into the structural constraints that influence the mapping process.  The key idea behind our approach is to decompose the mapping problem into smaller, more manageable subtasks, allowing for a systematic enumeration of all potential maps into a sphere. Through the careful consideration of topological and geometric constraints, we are able to construct a robust framework that can handle a wide range of input surfaces. Our methodology combines concepts from differential geometry, algebraic topology, and computational geometry to provide a comprehensive solution to this challenging problem.  Overall, our work contributes to the field of computational topology by presenting a systematic methodology for computing maps into a sphere. The developed algorithm offers a powerful tool for exploring the space of all possible mappings, thereby advancing our understanding of geometric structures and their relationships.

This study investigates the simplest Higgs-portal dark matter models, which propose that dark matter particles interact with normal matter solely through the Higgs field, a fundamental aspect of the Standard Model of particle physics. Recent results from the LUX and PandaX-II experiments have provided new insights into this paradigm, offering a unique opportunity to test the predictions of these models. The objective of this research is to analyze the latest data from these experiments and assess their implications for the simplest Higgs-portal dark matter models.  The analysis is based on a comprehensive review of the experimental data, including the results from the LUX-ZEPLIN (LUX) experiment's 2019 data release and the PandaX-II experiment's 2020 data release. The study employs a combination of statistical and machine learning techniques to identify potential signs of dark matter interactions in the data. The results show that the latest data from these experiments are consistent with the predictions of the simplest Higgs-portal dark matter models, providing strong evidence for their validity.  The key findings of this research indicate that the simplest Higgs-portal dark matter models are viable alternatives to more complex models, offering a promising avenue for understanding the nature of dark matter. The study's conclusions have significant implications for the development of future dark matter searches and the design of new experiments to detect dark matter particles. Overall, this research contributes to the ongoing quest to uncover the secrets of dark matter and its role in the universe.

This study explores the phenomenon of resistance without resistors, a seemingly anomalous occurrence that challenges conventional understanding of electrical resistance. Background research reveals that traditional models of electrical resistance rely on the presence of resistors, yet numerous instances of resistance without resistors have been documented in various fields, including physics, engineering, and materials science. The objective of this research is to investigate the underlying mechanisms and implications of this anomaly, shedding light on its causes, consequences, and potential applications.  Methodology involves a mixed-methods approach, combining theoretical analysis with experimental and simulation-based studies. Researchers employed advanced spectroscopic techniques to investigate the properties of materials exhibiting resistance without resistors, and performed simulations to model the behavior of electrical circuits in the absence of traditional resistors. Results show that the anomaly is not limited to specific materials or systems, but rather is a general property of certain types of electrical circuits.  Key findings indicate that resistance without resistors arises from the interaction between electromagnetic fields and the material's structure, rather than the presence of resistive components. This discovery has significant implications for the design and optimization of electrical circuits, as well as for our understanding of the fundamental laws of physics. The study concludes that the absence of resistors can be a deliberate design choice, rather than an anomaly, and that this approach can lead to novel solutions and applications in fields such as energy storage, electromagnetic shielding, and quantum computing.

Xenopus laevis embryos are renowned for their robust and reliable replication during early developmental stages. Understanding the mechanisms underlying this reliability, despite stochastic variations, provides insights into developmental biology's random-completion problem. This study aimed to elucidate the strategies employed by Xenopus embryos to ensure precise replication despite inherent randomness. We employed a combination of experimental embryology, live-cell imaging, and computational modeling to investigate the timing and coordination of DNA replication during early embryonic cell cycles. Our findings reveal that Xenopus embryos utilize a dynamic network of replication origins, coupled with a highly responsive checkpoint control system, to effectively manage replication timing. The spatial and temporal flexibility in origin activation compensates for intrinsic noise, ensuring complete and timely genome duplication. Furthermore, our computational models suggest that the balance between origin redundancy and efficient checkpoint responses minimizes the impact of random fluctuations, thus enhancing replication fidelity. These results demonstrate that the embryos mitigate the random-completion problem through a finely tuned balance of replication initiation and checkpoint mechanisms, which may constitute a universal strategy among rapidly developing systems. This work not only advances our understanding of embryonic development in Xenopus laevis but also offers broader implications for the study of stochastic processes in biological systems. Conclusively, the adaptive strategies of Xenopus embryos provide a model for investigating cellular mechanisms that achieve consistency amidst variability, with potential applications in addressing related challenges in synthetic biology and regenerative medicine.

We investigated the properties of a massive charged scalar field in the Kerr-Newman background, focusing on quasinormal modes, late-time tails, and stability. Through a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we derived a set of coupled differential equations that describe the evolution of the scalar field in the presence of a massive charge. By solving these equations, we obtained a detailed understanding of the quasinormal modes, which we found to be influenced by the mass of the scalar field and the charge of the black hole.  We also analyzed the late-time tails of the scalar field, which we found to be characterized by a power-law decay with a specific exponent that depends on the mass and charge of the scalar field. Furthermore, we examined the stability of the Kerr-Newman black hole in the presence of a massive charged scalar field, and found that the presence of the scalar field leads to a significant increase in the black hole's stability.  Our results provide new insights into the behavior of massive charged scalar fields in the Kerr-Newman background, and have implications for our understanding of the interplay between gravity, matter, and energy in extreme environments. The findings of this study can be used to inform future research on the properties of black holes and the behavior of scalar fields in the presence of strong gravity.

This paper proposes a novel watermarking technique for detecting integrity attacks on control systems using a Bernoulli-Gaussian physical watermark. Control systems are increasingly susceptible to integrity attacks that alter system behavior without causing noticeable changes in input-output data. Traditional methods of detecting such attacks rely on analyzing data statistics but fail to recognize subtle manipulations. Our approach introduces a non-intrusive watermark, inspired by the physical properties of water, to embed system-specific information as watermarks in the control signal. The watermark is generated based on a Bernoulli-Gaussian distribution and integrated into the control signal using a phase modulation method.  We evaluate the performance of our proposed watermarking technique using simulations of a nonlinear control system. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in detecting integrity attacks, even when they are barely perceptible in input-output data. We also study the resilience of the watermark to common noise sources and dynamic changes in control systems. The robustness of the proposed watermark under various conditions is shown to be superior to that of state-of-the-art techniques. This research extends the application of watermarking technology in control systems and provides a new perspective on designing effective attack detection mechanisms for industrial control systems.

In this study, we investigate Color Constancy by Learning to Predict Chromaticity from Luminance. Color constancy, the ability to perceive stable colors of objects under varying illuminations, is a crucial capability of the human visual system. Our work aims to address the challenges of color constancy in real-world scenarios by proposing a novel approach that leverages neural networks to learn chromaticity predictions from luminance values. By separating luminance and chromaticity information, our model can more accurately estimate the true colors of objects despite changes in lighting conditions.   Our results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms traditional color constancy algorithms and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmark datasets. The key idea behind our approach is to learn a mapping function between luminance and chromaticity, allowing the model to generalize well across different lighting conditions. We also provide insights into the learned representations, shedding light on how the network processes and interprets color information.   Overall, our study contributes to the field of color constancy by introducing a data-driven approach that enhances color perception under varying illuminants. By focusing on predicting chromaticity from luminance, our methodology offers a promising direction for improving color constancy algorithms in practical applications.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the $t \bar t hh \to t \bar t b \bar b bb\bar b$ channel as a promising probe for measuring di-Higgs physics. Our investigation aimed to explore the potential of this channel to constrain the parameter space of the Standard Model and beyond, particularly in the context of the Higgs boson's interactions with fermions and vector bosons.  Through a detailed simulation of the production and decay processes, we investigated the kinematic characteristics and backgrounds of the $t \bar t hh \to t \bar t b \bar b bb\bar b$ channel. Our results indicate that this channel can be a powerful tool for distinguishing di-Higgs signals from Standard Model backgrounds, with the potential to constrain the Higgs boson's trilinear coupling and other di-Higgs parameters.  We employed a combination of theoretical models, including the Standard Model, Next-to-Next-to-Loop (NNLL) QCD, and Next-to-Leading (NLO) electroweak corrections, to evaluate the production and decay rates of the $t \bar t hh$ and $b \bar b bb\bar b$ channels. Our analysis also incorporated a set of simulated di-Higgs signal events, generated using a combination of Monte Carlo generators and a custom implementation of the di-Higgs interactions.  Our findings demonstrate that the $t \bar t hh \to t \bar t b \bar b bb\bar b$ channel can provide a unique window into the di-Higgs sector, offering a promising avenue for the measurement of di-Higgs physics and the exploration of new physics beyond the Standard Model.

This research aims to simplify the list decoding process of Polar codes, a class of error-correcting codes known for their high efficiency and low decoding complexity. Traditional list decoding methods can be computationally intensive, especially as code length increases. The study introduces a novel approach called tree-pruning, which selectively removes unnecessary nodes from the decoding tree to reduce computational load while maintaining decoding accuracy.  The methodology involves developing an algorithm that identifies and prunes nodes based on their likelihood of contributing to the final decoding outcome. This pruning technique is integrated into the existing list decoding framework of Polar codes. Experimental evaluations were conducted using both theoretical models and practical simulations, comparing the performance of the original list decoding method with the proposed tree-pruning method.  Key findings indicate that the tree-pruning technique significantly reduces decoding complexity without compromising the error correction capability of Polar codes. Specifically, the pruning method achieves substantial reductions in computational time for large code lengths, demonstrating its effectiveness across various decoding scenarios.  In conclusion, this research successfully demonstrates that tree-pruning can effectively simplify the list decoding process of Polar codes, making it more scalable and efficient for real-world applications. Future work will focus on further optimizations and potential extensions of this approach to other types of error-correcting codes.

This research investigates the interstellar dust composition through the Fe K-edge, a key spectral feature that offers insights into the chemical and physical properties of dust particles in space. Background studies have shown that interstellar dust plays a crucial role in the formation of stars and planets, yet its composition and structure remain poorly understood. The Fe K-edge, a characteristic X-ray absorption peak, is particularly valuable for studying dust composition as it provides information on the presence of iron-rich species.   The objective of this study is to investigate the Fe K-edge in interstellar dust samples, with a focus on determining the abundance of iron-rich species and exploring their implications for our understanding of dust formation and evolution. To achieve this, we employed a combination of spectroscopic and computational methods, including X-ray spectroscopy and Monte Carlo simulations.   Our results indicate that the Fe K-edge in interstellar dust samples is characterized by a complex spectral profile, with multiple peaks and shoulders that are indicative of iron-rich species. The abundance of these species is found to be significant, with a range of iron oxides and silicates detected. The implications of these findings are significant, suggesting that iron-rich species play a crucial role in the formation and evolution of interstellar dust. The results of this study have important implications for our understanding of dust formation and evolution, and highlight the potential of the Fe K-edge as a diagnostic tool for studying interstellar dust composition.

We present a novel approach for the efficient discovery of ontology functional dependencies. Ontologies serve as crucial tools for knowledge representation in various domains. However, ensuring the integrity and quality of ontologies is essential for their effective utilization. Our work addresses the challenge of identifying functional dependencies within ontologies, which are pivotal for understanding the relationships and constraints among different concepts.  Through our proposed methodology, we introduce a scalable algorithm that can efficiently identify functional dependencies in ontologies. By leveraging the structural information embedded within ontologies, our approach can systematically detect dependencies among entities. We validated our method on a diverse set of ontologies from different domains and demonstrated its effectiveness in accurately capturing functional dependencies.  The results reveal a significant improvement in the efficiency and accuracy of ontology functional dependency discovery compared to existing techniques. Our approach offers a promising solution to enhance the quality and comprehensibility of ontologies by revealing hidden relationships among concepts. The implications of our work extend to various applications, including ontology alignment, data integration, and knowledge discovery.  In conclusion, our research contributes a valuable methodology for the automated discovery of ontology functional dependencies, paving the way for advancing the management and utilization of ontological knowledge structures.

In this study, we present a comprehensive analysis favoring the existence and characterization of the baryon resonance $N^*(1700)(3/2^-)$. This resonance, part of the nucleon excitation spectrum, has been a subject of debate due to its elusive nature in experimental observations and theoretical predictions. Our approach employs state-of-the-art partial wave analysis techniques alongside recent experimental data from photoproduction and hadron scattering experiments. By integrating lattice QCD calculations and incorporating quark model predictions, we refine our understanding of the resonance parameters, including mass, width, and decay modes.   Our results demonstrate a consistent extraction of the $N^*(1700)(3/2^-)$ parameters, providing strong evidence for its existence. This consistency is highlighted by the agreement between our refined parameter values and those predicted by quark model symmetries and recent lattice QCD simulations. Methodologically, we apply a coupled-channel formalism, enabling the disentanglement of overlapping resonances and reducing model-dependent ambiguities that have previously obscured the identification of this state.  These findings not only corroborate prior theoretical predictions but also underscore the significance of incorporating advanced computational techniques in resolving longstanding uncertainties in baryon spectroscopy. The identification and characterization of the $N^*(1700)(3/2^-)$ contribute to the broader understanding of the nucleon resonance landscape, offering potential implications for the study of quantum chromodynamics in the non-perturbative regime. We advocate for further experimental endeavors that target this specific resonance to validate our theoretical conclusions and enhance the precision of baryonic spectral analyses.

Diagonal Unloading Beamforming (DUB) emerges as a promising technique for enhancing source localization accuracy in complex acoustic environments. This research investigates the efficacy of DUB in identifying the precise origin of sound sources, particularly in scenarios involving interference and noise. The study's objective is to demonstrate how DUB can improve the resolution and robustness of conventional beamforming methods used in various applications, including sonar, radar, and wireless communications. Methodologically, the research employs simulations and empirical tests to compare DUB against traditional beamformers, such as the Minimum Variance Distortionless Response (MVDR) and Capon beamformers. By adjusting the diagonal loading parameter, DUB aims to balance interference suppression and noise reduction.  Key findings indicate that DUB significantly outperforms conventional techniques, particularly under scenarios characterized by high levels of spatial noise and limited sensor array elements. The adaptive modification of the beamforming matrix's diagonal elements provides substantial improvements in locating sources with higher accuracy and lower computational complexity. Furthermore, DUB demonstrates increased resilience to model mismatches and uncertainties in the propagation environment, essential for real-time and dynamic applications.  In conclusion, the study establishes DUB as a viable advancement in beamforming technology, offering superior localization precision and operational efficiency compared to existing methods. This research not only broadens the understanding of beamforming applications but also lays the groundwork for future explorations into adaptive and intelligent array processing systems. The results underscore the potential of DUB to revolutionize techniques employed in critical acoustic and electromagnetic source localization tasks.

Red clump stars, prominent in the Milky Way, serve as critical laboratories for studying stellar evolution and nucleosynthesis, particularly the phenomenon of extra-mixing. These stars, located on the horizontal branch of the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, provide insight into the processes that govern the mixing of stellar material during the advanced stages of star evolution. This research aims to investigate the mechanisms and consequences of extra-mixing in red clump stars by analyzing their elemental abundances and evolutionary paths. A combination of observational data from high-resolution spectroscopy and theoretical models was employed to ascertain the presence of extra-mixing and its impact on chemical composition. Key findings reveal a systematic variation in the abundance of certain elements, such as lithium and carbon, across different stellar populations, indicating that extra-mixing processes, including thermohaline mixing and rotationally-induced mixing, play a significant role in altering the chemical signature of these stars. Additionally, the results suggest a correlation between the intensity of extra-mixing and various parameters, including stellar mass and metallicity. In conclusion, red clump stars not only enhance our understanding of stellar dynamics but also provide essential clues regarding the broader implications of mixing processes in stellar evolution, offering a deeper understanding of the chemical enrichment of the Milky Way and the formation of its stellar populations. This study underscores the importance of red clump stars as key contributors to astrophysical research in nucleosynthesis and stellar physics.

The study of black hole stability under perturbations is critical in understanding their physical properties and evolution. In this research, we investigate the stability and quasinormal modes of black holes within the framework of the Tensor-Vector-Scalar (TeVeS) theory, focusing particularly on scalar field perturbations. TeVeS is an alternative to General Relativity that modifies gravitational interactions, necessitating a detailed examination of its implications on black hole dynamics. The objective of this study is to determine the stability characteristics of black holes under scalar perturbations and to explore the spectrum of quasinormal modes, which provide insights into the damping timescales and oscillation frequencies of these perturbations. Employing a linear perturbation analysis, we derive the equations governing scalar perturbations and solve them numerically to extract the quasinormal mode frequencies. Our findings reveal a spectrum of modes that are consistent with the expected stability for black holes in General Relativity, but with notable modifications in the frequencies and damping rates that reflect the unique features of TeVeS theory. These modifications imply potentially observable differences in the gravitational wave signals emitted by perturbed black holes, presenting a novel avenue for testing TeVeS theory through astrophysical observations. In conclusion, this research not only enhances our understanding of black hole stability in alternative theories of gravity but also proposes new methods to empirically distinguish such theories from General Relativity using gravitational wave astrophysics.

In the era of Software-Defined Internet of Vehicles (SDIoV), efficient query processing is a significant challenge due to the massive amount of real-time data generated by connected vehicles. Rule optimization plays a crucial role in ensuring the responsiveness and effectiveness of real-time query services in SDIoV systems. In this study, we explore several rule optimization techniques and their impact on the performance of rule-based query processing in real-time SDIoV applications.     Our experiments were conducted on a real-world SDIoV dataset containing over one million vehicle location updates per second. We evaluated the performance of three different rule optimization techniques 1) Static Rule Optimization (SRO), 2) Dynamic Rule Optimization (DRO), and 3) Hybrid Rule Optimization (HRO). The results demonstrated that HRO outperforms SRO and DRO by up to 40% in query response time and throughput. The hybrid approach combines the strengths of both static and dynamic optimization methods while minimizing their respective limitations.     We also explored the impact of rule complexity on the performance of each optimization method. Our findings showed that the performance benefits of rule optimization techniques were more pronounced for complex rules, highlighting their importance in real-world SDIoV applications where complex queries are common.     In conclusion, our research reveals the potential of rule optimization in improving the performance of real-time query services in SDIoV systems. We provide insights into the relative merits of different rule optimization techniques and their impact on the performance of real-time query processing. These findings can inform the design and implementation of rule-based query processing systems in future SDIoV applications, ensuring their responsiveness and effectiveness in managing the massive amounts of real-time data generated by connected vehicles. In today's interconnected world, understanding the intricacies of international trade flows is crucial for policymakers, businesses, and researchers. This study explores the multi-layer flow network of international trade using flow distances as a key metric. We begin by discussing the background and significance of international trade and the need for a more nuanced understanding of its complexities. Our objective is to develop a methodology for analyzing the multi-layer flow network of international trade and to identify the underlying patterns and structures. To achieve this, we employ a combination of network analysis techniques and gravity model-based approaches. We construct a multi-layer flow network, where each layer represents a different commodity, and calculate the flow distances between pairs of countries based on trade volumes. We then apply community detection algorithms and centrality measures to identify key regions and players in the network. Our key findings reveal that the multi-layer flow network of international trade exhibits complex structures, with several major trading blocs and key players playing pivotal roles. Furthermore, we find that flow distances can be used to identify hidden trade relationships and emerging trends in international trade. Our conclusion emphasizes the importance of considering multiple layers of international trade flows in any analysis and the potential implications for policy and business strategy. The multi-layer flow network of international trade reveals intricate patterns and structures that cannot be fully understood by analyzing trade flows in isolation. This study contributes to the ongoing debate in international economics by providing a novel perspective on the complexities of international trade and offering new insights into the underlying structures of global trade flows.

The circumgalactic medium (CGM) is the diffuse, ionized gas surrounding galaxies, playing a crucial role in regulating galaxy evolution. Despite its importance, the CGM's properties remain poorly understood, particularly in the context of galaxy-galaxy interactions and the interplay between simulations and observations. This study aims to investigate the properties of the CGM in simulations compared to observations, with a focus on the effects of numerical resolution, gas cooling, and galaxy interactions on the CGM's structure and composition.  Using a suite of high-resolution simulations of galaxy clusters, we examine the CGM's properties, including its temperature, density, and ionization state, as a function of galaxy mass, cluster mass, and numerical resolution. We compare our simulation results to observational data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the Chandra Deep Field South (CDFS). Our analysis reveals significant discrepancies between simulations and observations, particularly in the CGM's temperature and density profiles.  Our results suggest that simulations with higher numerical resolution and more realistic gas cooling schemes better reproduce the observed CGM properties. However, even with these improvements, simulations struggle to accurately capture the observed CGM's complex morphology and the effects of galaxy interactions on its structure. These findings highlight the need for further development of CGM models in simulations, with a focus on incorporating more realistic physics and observational constraints. By bridging the gap between simulations and observations, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of the CGM's role in regulating galaxy evolution and the intergalactic medium.

This research paper presents Minnorm, a novel algorithm designed to train over-parameterized deep neural networks effectively. The increasing complexity of deep neural networks has led to a surge in the number of model parameters, resulting in significant challenges for training, including vanishing gradients, exploding gradients, and slow convergence. Existing methods often rely on techniques such as weight decay, dropout, and batch normalization to mitigate these issues, but these approaches have limitations in handling large-scale deep networks.  The objective of this study is to develop an algorithm that can efficiently train over-parameterized deep neural networks by minimizing the magnitude of the model parameters. Minnorm is based on the idea of minimizing the minimum norm of the weight matrix, which has been shown to be a lower bound for the norm of the weight matrix. By iteratively updating the model parameters to minimize the minimum norm, Minnorm can effectively reduce the magnitude of the model parameters, leading to improved training stability and convergence.  The proposed algorithm is evaluated on several benchmark datasets, including ImageNet and CIFAR-10, and compared to state-of-the-art methods such as Adam and RMSProp. Experimental results show that Minnorm outperforms these methods in terms of training stability, convergence rate, and test accuracy. Specifically, Minnorm achieves state-of-the-art results on ImageNet with a top-1 accuracy of 92.5%, outperforming the best results reported in the literature. Overall, Minnorm provides a new approach to training over-parameterized deep neural networks and has the potential to improve the performance of deep learning models in various applications.

This study investigates threshold games on multiplayer graphs and examines their impact on cooperation among players. Threshold games, a well-known cooperative game model, are characterized by a threshold public good and a critical mass of players whose contribution is necessary to secure the public good. In this research, we analyze how threshold games behave on multiplayer graphs, a generalization of traditional graphs that represent pairwise relations between players. We consider two scenarios (1) when all players share a common threshold value, and (2) when each player has an individual threshold value. Through simulations, we observe that cooperation emerges more frequently in the second scenario compared to the first. Our results reveal that individual thresholds can lead to more diverse cooperative outcomes and can enhance the robustness of threshold games on multiplayer graphs.  Moreover, we explore how network structure influences the emergence of cooperation in threshold games. Specifically, we analyze three network structures random, small-world, and scale-free networks. The findings suggest that cooperation is more likely to emerge on small-world networks compared to the other two structures. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of these findings on the design of real-world systems, such as energy networks or communication systems, where cooperation among multiple agents is crucial.  In conclusion, this research contributes to the growing body of literature on threshold games and cooperation in complex networks. Our findings highlight the importance of individual thresholds and network structure in determining cooperative outcomes in threshold games on multiplayer graphs. These results may potentially inform the design of more effective and robust systems that rely on the cooperation of multiple agents.

In this work, we present a multiwavelength study of Swift GRB 060111B with the aim of constraining the origin of its prompt optical emission. By analyzing data from the Swift satellite, ground-based optical telescopes, and the Swift Ultra-Violet/Optical Telescope (UVOT), we investigate the characteristics of the prompt optical emission observed during the gamma-ray burst (GRB) event. Our analysis reveals a complex interplay between the X-ray and optical emission, suggesting that the prompt optical emission may arise from synchrotron radiation originating from relativistic electrons accelerated during the GRB event. We also examine the spectral energy distribution of the GRB and explore possible scenarios for the emission mechanisms responsible for the observed multiwavelength data. Through a combination of observational data and theoretical modeling, we aim to shed light on the physical processes governing the emission properties of GRB 060111B. Our findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge on the origins of prompt optical emission in GRBs and provide insights into the fundamental mechanisms at play during these energetic astrophysical events.

Inertial particles suspended in fluid flow exhibit complex behaviors that are crucial in various natural and industrial processes. In this study, we focus on the phenomenon of anisotropic clustering of inertial particles in homogeneous shear flow.   The objective of this research is to investigate how inertial particles interact and cluster under the influence of homogeneous shear flow with anisotropic characteristics.   Using computational fluid dynamics simulations coupled with Lagrangian particle tracking, we examine the motion and clustering tendencies of inertial particles in shear flows with varying degrees of anisotropy.  Our key findings reveal that inertial particles exhibit preferential clustering along certain directions dictated by the flow anisotropy, which significantly differs from isotropic flow conditions. Moreover, we observe the formation of elongated particle structures aligned with the flow direction due to shear-induced interactions.  In conclusion, our study sheds light on the intricate behavior of inertial particles in anisotropic shear flows, providing valuable insights for understanding and predicting particle dispersion, settling, and aggregation in real-world applications.

In this study, we investigate the implications of dark matter resolution on baryonic collapse in high-redshift simulations of the universe. Our aim is to elucidate the role that varying resolutions of dark matter, represented by particle mass and spatial resolution, play in accurately modeling baryonic structures during the epoch of reionization. We employ a set of cosmological hydrodynamical simulations with progressively refined dark matter resolution, maintaining consistent baryonic resolution parameters to isolate the effects attributable to dark matter. Our results indicate that higher dark matter resolution significantly enhances the fidelity of baryonic collapse, leading to more pronounced and accurately resolved structures. Specifically, we observe that with increased dark matter resolution, star-forming regions display higher densities and temperatures, which more closely align with observational constraints. Furthermore, we identify that low resolution in dark matter results in an underestimation of the gravitational potential wells, thereby delaying the onset and alteration of the nature of baryonic activity. These findings highlight the crucial sensitivity of baryonic processes to the resolution of dark matter in simulations, suggesting that accurately capturing early universe phenomena necessitates finer granularity of dark matter calculations. This work emphasizes that future simulations aimed at examining the intricacies of baryonic matter collapse, particularly in the context of cosmic dawn and the buildup of primordial galaxies, must consider dark matter to a higher precision to avoid significant inaccuracies. Our methodology underscores the interconnectedness of dark matter treatment with baryonic dynamics and informs the design of next-generation cosmological models.

Disordered alloys, characterized by the random distribution of constituent elements, present unique challenges in predicting electronic properties due to their inherent structural complexity. This research examines lattice charge models and their efficacy in calculating core level shifts within such alloys. The objective is to establish a more precise understanding of the electronic structure modifications induced by disorder and compositional variance. Our methodology integrates advanced computational techniques, including density functional theory (DFT), combined with lattice charge simulations to rigorously evaluate core level shifts. We analyze multiple alloy systems, varying in composition and disorder degree, to discern patterns and correlations between electronic structure perturbations and material properties. Key findings reveal that lattice charge models offer enhanced predictive accuracy for core level shifts compared to traditional approaches, addressing the asymmetries and local environmental effects typical in disordered alloys. The study further identifies critical factors influencing charge redistribution, such as local atomic environments and alloying element electronegativity differences. These insights enable the development of robust predictive models, facilitating better material design and alloy engineering. In conclusion, the integration of lattice charge models with core level shift analysis provides a significant advancement in the predictive modeling of electronic properties in disordered alloys, contributing to the broader understanding of material behaviors at an atomic level. This approach opens new avenues for tailoring electronic properties through compositional engineering, with implications for the development of advanced materials for technological applications.

In this study, we perform an extensive broadband photometric reverberation mapping analysis on a significant sample of quasars located within the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Reverberation Mapping (SDSS-RM) project and the Stripe 82 region. Our primary objective is to enhance the temporal accuracy of measuring time lags between variable continuum and emission line fluxes, which are crucial parameters in determining the size and structure of the broad-line region (BLR) in quasars. By utilizing high-cadence photometric data, we employ a multiscale autoregressive model to deconvolve light curves, effectively isolating significant intrinsic quasar variability signals. Our results notably improve upon prior determinations of BLR sizes, offering expanded spatial correlations through a robust reverberation mapping framework that mitigates aliasing and seasonal sampling gaps. The analysis reveals a consistent relationship between BLR sizes and luminosity across varying quasar luminosities and redshifts, aligning with theoretical predictions under the virial assumption. Furthermore, our research elucidates the potential of broadband photometry as a cost-effective alternative to spectroscopic reverberation mapping, proposing its integration in future large-scale surveys. Key methodologies include cross-correlation analysis refined for enhanced sensitivity in light curve synchronization and detailed statistical techniques to address noise interference. This approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of quasar dynamics but also propels the advancement of photometric monitoring techniques. Our findings provide substantive contributions to the field of active galactic nuclei studies, propelling forward initiatives aimed at mapping out cosmic distances with greater precision. The implications of this work are anticipated to be foundational for next-generation astronomical observations and quasar-based cosmological investigations.

This study explores the thermal properties of supernova matter, specifically focusing on the bulk homogeneous phase. The key objective is to investigate the temperature-dependent behavior of supernova matter to enhance our understanding of the dynamics and evolution of these energetic stellar events. By conducting extensive molecular dynamics simulations, we elucidate the thermal conductivity, specific heat capacity, and thermal expansion of the bulk homogeneous phase of supernova matter. Our results reveal intricate temperature dependencies for these thermal properties, shedding light on how heat is transferred and stored within such extreme astrophysical environments.  The problem addressed in this work revolves around the necessity to comprehend the thermal characteristics of supernova matter, given its critical role in the explosion mechanisms and subsequent nucleosynthesis processes. By unraveling the thermal properties of the bulk homogeneous phase, we strive to provide valuable insights into the overall thermodynamic behavior of supernovae, offering crucial information for astrophysical models and theoretical predictions.  The methodology employed involves utilizing molecular dynamics simulations with state-of-the-art potential energy models to replicate the extreme conditions present in supernovae. By systematically varying the temperature and analyzing the resulting thermal properties, we gain a comprehensive understanding of how heat is managed and propagated within the bulk homogeneous phase of supernova matter. These findings contribute to the broader field of astrophysics by enriching our knowledge of the intricacies of stellar explosions and their thermal evolution.

This study presents an ALMA (Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array) survey targeting CO emission lines in submillimetre galaxies (SMGs), focusing on understanding their companions, potential triggering mechanisms, and the environmental context within blended sources. We employed ALMA's high sensitivity and angular resolution to detect CO line emissions in SMGs, allowing us to probe the interstellar medium and identify associated molecular gas structures. Our analysis reveals that SMGs frequently have companion galaxies, indicating possible environmental influences such as ram-pressure stripping or tidal interactions that could trigger star formation. Additionally, we observed several SMGs blended with other compact sources, suggesting that these sources might be interacting or merging. By analyzing the CO line fluxes and velocity widths, we infer that the triggering of star formation in SMGs could be driven by mergers or galactic encounters. The key methodologies include detailed spectral line mapping, robust source separation techniques, and multi-wavelength data integration. Our findings contribute to our understanding of the formation and evolution of SMGs within their host environments, providing insights into the role of environmental factors in shaping galaxy properties.

This study examines the performance of the Distributed Channel Allocation and Scheduling (DISH) protocol in supporting multi-channel MAC (Media Access Control) protocols for wireless networks. Background research reveals that wireless networks face significant challenges in efficiently utilizing multiple channels, leading to increased congestion, reduced throughput, and decreased overall network performance. The DISH protocol, designed to optimize channel allocation and scheduling, has garnered attention as a potential solution. However, its suitability for multi-channel MAC protocols remains unexplored.  The objective of this research is to investigate the performance of DISH in supporting multi-channel MAC protocols, with a focus on its ability to manage channel allocation, scheduling, and resource utilization. A comprehensive simulation-based approach is employed to evaluate the performance of DISH in various network scenarios, including different channel configurations, traffic patterns, and network sizes.  The results of this study demonstrate that DISH can effectively support multi-channel MAC protocols, achieving improved channel utilization, reduced congestion, and increased throughput compared to traditional single-channel MAC protocols. Key findings indicate that DISH's ability to adapt to changing network conditions and optimize channel allocation leads to significant performance gains. The study also highlights the importance of considering channel allocation and scheduling in multi-channel MAC protocols, and provides insights into the design and optimization of such protocols. Overall, this research contributes to the understanding of DISH's potential in supporting multi-channel MAC protocols, and has implications for the development of more efficient and effective wireless networks.

In our study, we present a comprehensive analysis of the giant molecular cloud (GMC) W 37, utilizing high-resolution data from both ground-based and space observatories. Our investigation aims to unravel the structural complexities and star-forming capabilities intrinsic to W 37, a prominent assembly within the Milky Way's constellation standing as a candidate for stellar genesis mechanisms. Through careful examination of the atomic and molecular gas distributions, we identified several dense cores, within which prestellar conditions appear favorable. By implementing spectral line mapping techniques alongside CO isotopologue measurements, we quantified the mass, temperature gradients, and kinematic features that define the cloud's architecture. This approach allowed us to ascertain the extent of turbulence and its role in star formation efficiency. Moreover, we applied hierarchical bayesian models to evaluate the influence of external Galactic forces on the cloud's dynamics. Our findings highlight significant variations in gas density that align with enhanced accretion zones, likely triggered by external perturbations. Notably, our study also recorded distinct velocity dispersions that challenge existing paradigms of uniform core-to-envelope transitions in similar GMCs. These results contribute to refining theoretical models that predict star formation rates and initial mass functions in molecular clouds. We propose that W 37 serves as a critical laboratory for studying star formation's dependency on environmental factors, providing insights that may be extrapolated to infer Galactic evolution models. Collectively, our work underscores the intricacy of GMCs and underscores the need for further integrative studies to elucidate star-forming dynamics within such entities.

In the study of strong interactions under extreme conditions, the dissociation of pions and kaons in hot, dense quark matter plays a critical role in understanding the behavior of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) and the evolution of heavy-ion collisions. This research aims to investigate the Mott dissociation of these mesonic states as a function of temperature and baryon density, contributing to the theoretical framework surrounding the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) phase. Utilizing a combination of lattice QCD calculations and effective field theoretical models, we analyze the mass variations of pions and kaons within quark matter, demonstrating how their binding energies change under extreme thermal and chemical conditions. Our findings reveal that both pions and kaons undergo Mott dissociation at significantly different temperature thresholds, influenced by the density of the medium. In particular, we observe that kaons exhibit a higher Mott dissociation temperature compared to pions, consistent with their distinct quark content and interactions. Importantly, this study highlights the implications of mesonic dissociation on the dynamics of the QGP and its experimental signatures, advocating for enhanced detection strategies in high-energy particle collisions. Overall, our results contribute to a deeper understanding of the phase structure of QCD matter and offer crucial insights for future investigations into the properties of the early universe conditions created in heavy-ion collisions, facilitating novel experimental and theoretical approaches in the field.

In this work, we investigate the entropy properties of the convolution of Gibbs probabilities on the circle, focusing on deriving a comprehensive formula that characterizes these entropic dynamics. The ubiquitous presence of Gibbs distributions in statistical mechanics and information theory, coupled with the non-trivial geometry of the circle, necessitates a deeper understanding of the entropy associated with their convolutions. Our primary contribution is the formulation of an explicit expression for the entropy of the convolution of two Gibbs measures, which we achieve by employing tools from harmonic analysis and probability theory. We utilize the Fourier transform to reinterpret the convolution operation in frequency space, enabling us to circumvent the complications arising from the circular topology. Our findings reveal that the entropy of the resulting measure depends intricately on the interacting potentials governing the original Gibbs distributions. We demonstrate that our formula extends classical results from linear spaces to the circular setting, thereby filling a significant gap in the theoretical framework of probabilistic convolution on compact groups. Furthermore, through rigorous numerical simulations, we validate our theoretical predictions and demonstrate the applicability of our results to practical scenarios involving data with cyclical nature. This work advances the theoretical understanding of entropy in cyclic systems and opens avenues for further research into more general compact manifolds, which hold promise for advancements in fields such as statistical mechanics, machine learning, and cryptographic algorithms.

Pulsed lasers have emerged as a promising tool for mitigating the ever-growing space debris issue. This study investigates the effects of pulsed laser interaction with different target shapes of space debris spherical, cylindrical, and flat. Experiments were conducted using a NdYAG pulsed laser (1064 nm, 6 ns pulse width) at various pulse energies (0.2-5.4 J). The interaction process was characterized through measurement of the debris' mass changes and the generation of secondary debris. Spherical targets underwent ablation leading to fragmentation, producing larger and more numerous secondary debris than cylindrical and flat targets. The latter two shapes presented less fragmentation, leading to a reduction in secondary debris. The findings demonstrate that target shape significantly influences the efficiency and safety of pulsed laser interactions with space debris. These results contribute to the ongoing research aimed at developing effective debris mitigation strategies for space missions.

We investigate the problem of scheduling wireless links in the physical interference model using fractional edge coloring. Our work aims to efficiently assign time slots to communication links in wireless networks to minimize interference and maximize overall network throughput. By leveraging fractional edge coloring, we propose a novel approach that optimally schedules the links while considering the physical constraints of interference between neighboring links.   Our results demonstrate that the proposed fractional edge coloring technique outperforms existing scheduling methods in terms of minimizing interference and improving network throughput. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive simulations on various network topologies, showcasing the superiority of our scheduling algorithm in achieving better link scheduling outcomes.  Key ideas in our work include formulating the link scheduling as a fractional edge coloring problem and designing an efficient algorithm to solve it. Our methodology involves modeling the interference constraints between links and developing a scheduling algorithm that optimally assigns time slots to wireless links. By integrating these components, we achieve a scheduling solution that efficiently manages interference in wireless networks. Our study contributes to advancing the field of link scheduling in wireless networks by providing a practical and effective fractional edge coloring-based approach for optimizing link scheduling in the physical interference model.

This research focuses on the direct measurement of low-energy $^{22}$Ne(p,$\gamma$)$^{23}$Na resonances, providing a detailed analysis of the nuclear reaction process. The study employs high-resolution gamma-ray spectroscopy with a high-purity germanium detector to measure the energy levels and decay patterns of the excited states in the daughter nucleus, $^{23}$Na. The objective was to accurately determine the resonance energies and corresponding probabilities, which are essential parameters for understanding the transfer of nucleons in light nuclei. The methodology involved precise control over beam energy and intensity, as well as extensive data acquisition and analysis using sophisticated software to isolate the characteristic gamma rays emitted during the pion capture process. Key findings include the identification of multiple low-lying excited states in $^{23}$Na and the determination of their respective lifetimes, contributing significantly to our knowledge of the nuclear structure of light nuclei. The results of this study enhance theoretical models of nuclear reactions and provide valuable insights into the dynamics of nucleon transfer reactions.
