This phenomenon is thought to be driven by the interaction between the expanding supernova shockwave and the surrounding circumstellar medium.  The objective of this research was to investigate the relationship between dust and the plateau phase of a Type II-Plateau supernova, with a focus on the 2004dj event. A comprehensive analysis of archival data, including optical and near-infrared observations, was conducted to determine the properties of the circumstellar dust shell surrounding the supernova.  The results of this study indicate that the dust shell surrounding 2004dj was composed of silicate-rich grains with a median size of approximately 1.5 microns. The dust shell was found to be optically thick, with a visual extinction of A_V = 2.5, and was characterized by a complex structure, with multiple layers and a prominent dust lane. The interaction between the supernova shockwave and the dust shell was found to be responsible for the prolonged plateau phase, with the dust shell serving as a reservoir for the release of energy.  The key findings of this study highlight the importance of dust in shaping the evolution of Type II-Plateau supernovae, and demonstrate the potential for dust to influence the timing and duration of the plateau phase. The results of this research provide new insights into the complex interactions between supernovae and their surroundings, and have significant implications for our understanding of the physics of these events.

Studying the radial distributions of main-sequence components in young massive star clusters provides valuable insights into their formation and evolution processes. NGC 1856, a prominent young massive star cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, offers a unique opportunity to investigate the spatial arrangement of its main-sequence components.   This research aims to analyze the radial distributions of the two main-sequence components in the young massive star cluster NGC 1856 to understand the spatial configuration of these components within the cluster.   Utilizing high-resolution observational data from advanced telescopes, we conducted a systematic analysis of the main-sequence stars in NGC 1856. By employing statistical methods and analytical tools, we quantitatively examined the radial distributions of the main-sequence components.   Our results reveal distinct radial distributions of the two main-sequence components in NGC 1856, indicating possible variations in their formation mechanisms and dynamical evolution within the cluster. The inner and outer regions of the cluster exhibit different characteristics in terms of main-sequence component distribution, suggesting complex dynamical processes at play.   The radial distributions of the main-sequence components in the young massive star cluster NGC 1856 provide important clues about the cluster's past interactions, stellar dynamics, and evolutionary history. This study enhances our understanding of the formation and development of massive star clusters in the context of galactic star formation.

The Ni2Mn1.4In0.6 Heusler alloy, a member of the magnetic shape memory (MSME) family, exhibits unique properties due to its adaptive magnetic modulation behavior. In the background section, we discuss the fundamental concepts of magnetic shape memory alloys and their applications. The objective of this study is to investigate the adaptive magnetic modulation in Ni2Mn1.4In0.6 through magnetization measurements under different temperature and magnetic field conditions. The methodology used includes magnetization measurements using a vibrating sample magnetometer.  Our key findings reveal that Ni2Mn1.4In0.6 undergoes reversible martensitic transformation below its Curie temperature, accompanied by significant changes in its magnetic properties. The adaptive magnetic modulation behavior is observed through the hysteresis loops, which exhibit large coercive forces and magnetoelastic coupling effects. Furthermore, the transformation temperatures are strongly influenced by the applied magnetic field and temperature conditions, demonstrating the alloy's excellent adaptive capabilities.  The conclusion emphasizes the significance of our findings, as they provide insights into the complex magnetic behavior of Ni2Mn1.4In0.6 and highlight its potential as a versatile adaptive magnetic material for various applications, such as sensors, actuators, and energy storage devices. The results of this study extend the understanding of magnetic shape memory alloys and contribute to the ongoing research and development efforts in this field.

Ultracold two-dimensional (2D) Bose gases have emerged as a unique platform for exploring quantum phenomena, offering insights into low-dimensional physics. Despite extensive studies, the role of correlation effects in such systems remains an area of active research. This study aims to elucidate the impact of interparticle correlations on the properties of 2D Bose gases at ultracold temperatures. By employing advanced theoretical frameworks and numerical simulations, we examine the phase behavior and coherence properties of these systems. Our methodology includes utilizing the Bogoliubov theory alongside quantum Monte Carlo simulations to analyze the role of correlations, particularly in close vicinity to the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition. Key findings reveal that correlations significantly influence the superfluid density and momentum distribution, leading to observable modifications in both macroscopic and microscopic properties of the system. Evidence of enhanced correlation effects near the critical temperature highlights the importance of these interactions in dictating the observed quantum phase transitions. Our study provides a detailed characterization of correlation effects, contributing to the fundamental understanding of 2D Bose gases. This enhanced comprehension not only impacts theoretical physics but also has implications for experimental pursuits in quantum simulation, where fine-tuning interactions could unveil novel phases of matter. Conclusively, our work underscores the pivotal role of correlation effects, advocating for their consideration in future explorations of ultracold 2D systems.

This study investigates the consistent searches for Supersymmetric Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) effects within non-resonant dijet events. The primary objective is to detect potential signals of new physics beyond the Standard Model through the analysis of high-energy dijet production processes. We employ advanced Monte Carlo simulation techniques to model various scenarios that could manifest as SMEFT signatures in dijet events. Our methodology involves rigorous data analysis using cutting-edge statistical methods to ensure robust extraction of signal parameters. The results indicate significant deviations from background expectations in certain regions of parameter space, suggesting the presence of SMEFT effects. This work not only contributes to our understanding of dijet production mechanisms but also provides valuable insights into the feasibility of detecting new physics through these channels. Key methodologies include the application of likelihood ratio tests and the utilization of machine learning algorithms to enhance detection efficiency. These findings underscore the importance of ongoing searches for SMEFT signals in dijet events as they offer promising avenues for probing fundamental interactions and particle physics beyond the Standard Model.

The abstract focuses on the study of the mass distribution of companions orbiting low-mass white dwarfs (LMWDs). Historically, the detection of these companions has been challenging due to their small masses and proximity to their parent stars. This research aims to explore the mass range and orbital characteristics of these companions by leveraging advanced spectroscopic techniques and high-resolution imaging data.  Utilizing the Keck Observatory and the Hubble Space Telescope, the study targets LMWDs within the Galactic field and nearby star-forming regions. By analyzing the radial velocity variations induced by the gravitational pull of the companions, the mass limits of potential companions could be determined. Additionally, multi-object spectroscopy allows for the identification of multiple companions in a single observation.  Key findings include the discovery of companions with masses ranging from Earth to Neptune-like planets, orbiting at distances that suggest they formed independently of the LMWDs. The study also reveals that some companions exhibit eccentric orbits, indicating past interactions with other bodies. These results contribute to our understanding of planet formation processes around low-mass stellar remnants and provide insights into the evolution of planetary systems over cosmic time.

This study investigates the fraction of thermal Comptonized photons that return to impinge on the soft source within neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs), a critical aspect in understanding energy feedback mechanisms. The objective is to utilize a Monte Carlo simulation approach to estimate the extent of this back-impact phenomenon, given its implications on the thermal state and emission spectra of neutron star accretion environments. The methodology involved simulating photon trajectories and interactions in a model LMXB system, using Monte Carlo techniques to track the paths of Comptonized photons in a stratified plasma environment. Key variables, such as electron temperature and optical depth, were varied systematically to gauge their influence on photon feedback rates. The findings reveal that a significant fraction of Comptonized photons do indeed return to the soft source, with the percentage heavily dependent on the optical depth and electron distribution parameters. For realistic parameter settings, up to 20% of these modified photons reverse course, suggesting that a considerable amount of energy is redirected back into the accretion disk or neutron star surface. The simulations highlight the importance of accounting for photon feedback in modeling the energy balance and spectral characteristics of LMXBs. This study concludes that the Monte Carlo method provides a robust tool for quantifying photon feedback and can effectively aid in refining theoretical models of neutron star accretion physics, thus enhancing our understanding of the interactions between Comptonization processes and thermal emissions in these unique astrophysical systems.

We investigated the evolution of the GeV spectrum in Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) from the prompt phase to the afterglow stage, focusing on the 160509A event. Through a comprehensive analysis of data from the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope and the Swift XRT, we explored the temporal and spectral characteristics of the GeV emission.  Our results indicate that the GeV spectrum of GRB 160509A underwent a significant evolution from the prompt phase to the afterglow stage, characterized by a transition from a hard, power-law spectrum to a softer, exponential decay spectrum. This transition occurred approximately 10 hours after the burst onset, coinciding with the onset of the afterglow phase.  We employed a combination of spectral and temporal analysis techniques to disentangle the prompt and afterglow components. Our findings suggest that the GeV emission in the afterglow stage is dominated by synchrotron radiation from a shock wave propagating through the circumgalactic medium. We also detected a significant correlation between the GeV flux and the X-ray flux, indicating a common physical mechanism driving both the prompt and afterglow emission.  Our study provides new insights into the complex evolution of the GeV spectrum in GRBs and highlights the importance of multi-messenger observations in understanding the physics of these extreme events. The results of this analysis contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms driving the afterglow emission and shed light on the role of the circumgalactic medium in shaping the spectral evolution of GRBs.

The Interstellar Medium (ISM) plays a crucial role in the evolution of stars, especially the early stages where mass accretion and outflows occur. The far-infrared spectral energy distribution (SED) of Protostellar Protoclusters (PPCs) provides essential information on the ISM properties. ISM modeling around Protostellar Nebulae (PPNs), which represents the earliest stage of star formation, remains a challenging task due to the complexity of gas dynamics and the uncertain physical conditions.   Our objective is to remodel the envelope around IRAS 07134+1005, a PPN candidate, using a multi-component ISM model and the observed far-infrared SED. We aim to investigate the physical conditions, gas surfaces, and abundances of key molecules within this envelope.   We employ a multi-component ISM model based on the radiative transfer code MARCS and the chemical modeling code UDfitted, combining the optically thin gas emission with the optically thick dust emission. The ISM model includes various gas components like molecular hydrogen, HII regions, and warm dust. We analyze the observational data of IRAS 07134+1005 from the Infrared Space Observatory (ISO) and the Herschel Space Observatory, taking into account the uncertainties in the data.   Our results reveal that the envelope around IRAS 07134+1005 has a complex structure with multiple gas components. The inner envelope contains warm molecular hydrogen, dust, and HII regions, while the outer envelope consists of cold molecular hydrogen and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). We find that the observed emission features in the far-infrared SED can be explained by the presence of warm carbon monoxide, which originates from the shocked gas surrounding the protostar. Furthermore, we detect water vapor in the warm inner envelope, which is crucial for understanding the water delivery to the forming planetary system.   Our study successfully remodels the envelope around the PPN candidate IRAS 07134+1005 using a multi-component ISM model and observational data. The findings provide valuable insights into the physical conditions, gas surfaces, and abundances

This research paper provides a theoretical description of the gamma-ray burst (GRB) 160625B event with a focus on the transition from a wind environment to the interstellar medium (ISM) and its implications for a magnetized outflow. The objective of the study is to investigate the dynamics and evolution of the GRB 160625B event during this transition phase. The methodology involves numerical simulations based on magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) equations to model the behavior of the outflow as it propagates through varying environments.   Key findings reveal that the interaction between the wind and the ISM plays a critical role in shaping the outflow properties, leading to complex magnetic field configurations and energy dissipation processes. The transition zone exhibits distinct observational signatures that can help distinguish between different outflow models. Furthermore, the presence of a magnetized outflow affects the overall energy distribution and particle acceleration mechanisms within the GRB system.  In conclusion, this study sheds light on the importance of considering the wind-to-ISM transition in understanding the behavior of magnetized outflows in GRBs, providing valuable insights for future observational and theoretical studies in high-energy astrophysics.

The accelerating universe is a phenomenon observed in the late 1990s, where the expansion of the universe is no longer slowing down, but is instead speeding up. This acceleration is attributed to two main components the variation of the gravitational constant (G) and the cosmological constant (Λ). The variation of G and Λ with time has been a subject of intense debate and research, with several models proposed to explain this phenomenon.   This study aims to investigate the effects of time-varying G and Λ on the accelerating universe. We explore the possibility of a non-constant gravitational force and the variation of the cosmological constant with time, and their impact on the evolution of the universe.   Using a combination of theoretical models and numerical simulations, we analyze the effects of time-varying G and Λ on the acceleration of the universe. Our results show that the variation of G and Λ with time can lead to a more rapid acceleration of the universe, with significant implications for our understanding of the cosmos.   Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the variation of G and Λ can also affect the formation and evolution of structure within the universe, with potential implications for the distribution of galaxies and galaxy clusters.   In conclusion, this study provides new insights into the accelerating universe, highlighting the importance of considering time-varying G and Λ in our understanding of the cosmos. Our findings suggest that a more dynamic and evolving universe may be required to explain the observed acceleration, and we propose further research into this area to better understand the underlying mechanisms.

The phenomenon of Zipf's law, characterized by a power-law distribution with a slope of approximately -1, is often observed in natural and social systems. This research explores the robustness of scaling behaviors in sample space reducing (SSR) processes, elucidating its fundamental role in the manifestation of Zipf's law within diffusion dynamics on directed networks. Our objective is to uncover how SSR processes inherently facilitate the emergence of this empirical law within networked systems characterized by directed pathways, which are pivotal in numerous applications ranging from sociology to information sciences. Employing both analytical and computational methods, we examine directed network models where diffusion processes are constrained by SSR dynamics. Our approach involves systematically quantifying the distribution patterns that emerge under various structural and dynamic conditions. Key findings reveal that scaling laws, particularly Zipf's law, exhibit remarkable resilience across a diverse array of directed network configurations when SSR mechanisms are operational. This robustness suggests a general principle underpinning the appearance of Zipf's law, irrespective of the network specifics or external perturbations. The research highlights that SSR processes, by limiting the exploration of sample spaces during diffusion, naturally skew the frequency distributions toward Zipfian behavior. In conclusion, our study substantiates that the extreme robustness of scaling in SSR processes offers a compelling explanatory framework for the prevalence of Zipf's law in directed network scenarios, providing insights with significant theoretical and practical implications regarding systemic organization and information diffusion.

This work presents a novel approach for image deblurring and super-resolution by leveraging adaptive sparse domain selection and adaptive regularization techniques. The primary goal of our research is to enhance the quality of blurred and low-resolution images by effectively incorporating sparse representations and regularization methods. Through extensive experimentation on various benchmark datasets, we have demonstrated significant improvements in image quality in terms of sharpness, clarity, and detail preservation.  Our approach addresses the challenges posed by blurred and low-resolution images by adaptively selecting the most suitable sparse domain representation for each image patch. By dynamically adjusting the regularization parameters based on the characteristics of the image content, we mitigate artifacts and noise amplification commonly associated with traditional deblurring and super-resolution algorithms. This adaptive framework allows for robust performance across a wide range of image types and degradation levels.  Key contributions of our work include the development of an efficient optimization framework that jointly optimizes sparse domain selection and regularization parameters, leading to superior image reconstruction results. The methodology is founded on the principles of sparsity and regularization, enhancing the ability to restore intricate image details while suppressing artifacts. Overall, our approach offers a promising solution for image deblurring and super-resolution tasks, showcasing advancements in adaptive sparse domain selection and regularization for improved image quality.

This research paper explores the implementation of turbulence transport within the CRONOS (Coupled Radiation and Optics in Nonlinear Space) framework to enhance the simulation of coronal mass ejections (CMEs). Initially, the background establishes the importance of accurately modeling CME propagation, which involves complex interactions with solar plasma and magnetic fields. The objective of this study was to integrate turbulence into CRONOS, aiming to improve the realism and predictive accuracy of CME simulations.  Methodologically, the study involved extending CRONOS by incorporating turbulent transport equations that account for ion-neutral collisions, thermal conduction, and magnetic field fluctuations. This enhancement was tested using a suite of numerical experiments, including both idealized scenarios and those based on real solar data. Key findings indicated that the inclusion of turbulence significantly improved the simulation of CME evolution, particularly in capturing the acceleration and deceleration phases of CMEs. Additionally, the model demonstrated better agreement with observed CME properties, such as their speed and directionality.  The results highlight the necessity of considering turbulence in models of CME propagation. The enhanced realism provided by the integrated turbulence transport mechanism suggests that future CME simulations could benefit from incorporating these effects. In conclusion, this work contributes valuable insights into the dynamics of CMEs and supports the development of more accurate space weather prediction tools.

In this study, we investigate the high-gravity spreading behavior of liquid coatings on wetting flexible substrates, addressing the challenges associated with uniform coating application in variable gravitational conditions. We employed a combination of experimental techniques and numerical simulations to analyze the dynamics of liquid spreading on polymeric substrates with different wettability properties. Our results reveal that elevated gravitational forces significantly enhance the spreading rate and uniformity of the coatings, yielding a more consistent application across varying substrate geometries. We systematically varied the liquid viscosities and substrate flexibilities to identify optimal conditions for achieving desired coating thicknesses and uniform coverage.   Notably, we formulated a dimensionless parameter that characterizes the combined effects of gravitational forces, surface tension, and substrate flexibility, facilitating a predictive framework for the coating process. Through comprehensive data analysis, we established a relationship between the spreading kinetics and the physical properties of the liquids and substrates, which enables better control over the application process in industrial settings.   Our findings contribute to the existing body of knowledge by providing insights into the intricate interplay between gravitational forces and the physical characteristics of flexible substrates, proposing novel strategies for enhancing coating processes in various applications, including electronics, textiles, and biomedical devices. This work lays the groundwork for future research aimed at optimizing coating techniques under diverse operational conditions, ultimately improving product performance and durability.

In this work, we investigate the theoretical framework of Gravi-Natural Higgs (GNH) within the context of conformal new physics. Our primary aim is to reconcile the Standard Model's hierarchy problem with gravitational effects while exploring the implications of conformal symmetry. We formulate a comprehensive model that incorporates a scalar field exhibiting properties akin to the Higgs mechanism, yet intertwined with gravitational interactions that emerge naturally in a higher-dimensional spacetime. By employing a combination of renormalization group techniques and effective field theory principles, we derive the criteria for achieving electroweak symmetry breaking via conformal dynamics.  Results show that finite contributions to mass scales arise in a controlled manner, mitigating the issues tied to quantum corrections that plague traditional Higgs scenarios. We confirm that this approach leads to a minimal fine-tuning requirement, thereby providing a potentially elegant solution to the fine-tuning problem. Additionally, we analyze the stability and phenomenological consequences of the GNH framework, advancing our understanding of the resulting particle spectrum and interactions. Specific attention is given to the implications for gravitational waves and their signatures in cosmological contexts.   Our findings suggest that the interplay between gravity and conformal invariance paves the way for novel insights in high-energy physics, indicating a pathway to probe this rich theoretical landscape through upcoming experiments. Overall, we posit that Gravi-Natural Higgs models, underpinned by conformal symmetries, may significantly contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of fundamental forces and particles in the universe.

In this research, we investigate the problem of barter exchange with multiple items per agent within the context of tropical vertex-disjoint cycles in a vertex-colored digraph. Our study aimed to address the challenge of finding optimal exchange cycles in a system where agents possess multiple items and engage in transactions based on their individual preferences. By formulating the exchange process as a vertex-colored digraph, we were able to model the interactions between agents and the items they possess, considering both the combinatorial aspects of the items and the structural constraints of the cycles. Through our proposed methodology, which combines techniques from graph theory, combinatorial optimization, and tropical algebra, we were able to demonstrate the existence of tropical vertex-disjoint cycles that facilitate efficient barter exchanges among agents with multiple items. The results of our study provide insights into the fundamental properties of tropical cycles in vertex-colored digraphs and offer a novel approach to optimizing barter exchanges in complex economic systems. Our findings contribute to the theoretical understanding of combinatorial optimization problems in network structures and have implications for the design of efficient exchange mechanisms in multi-agent systems with diverse preferences and transactional capacities.

We investigated the presence and characteristics of overtone and multi-mode RR Lyrae stars in the globular cluster M3, utilizing a combination of photometric and spectroscopic observations. Through a thorough analysis of 245 RR Lyrae stars, we identified 44 overtone and 21 multi-mode stars, representing a significant fraction of the cluster's RR Lyrae population. Our results suggest that the observed overtone and multi-mode stars are not merely artifacts of the photometric data, but rather genuine stars with distinct properties.  We employed a Bayesian approach to model the cluster's RR Lyrae period-luminosity relation, incorporating the overtone and multi-mode stars to refine the model. Our findings indicate that the inclusion of these stars significantly improves the model's fit to the observed data, suggesting that they play a crucial role in understanding the cluster's RR Lyrae evolution.  Key to our analysis was the development of a new spectroscopic classification scheme for RR Lyrae stars, which enabled us to accurately identify overtone and multi-mode stars. We also applied a novel method for estimating the effective temperatures of these stars, which revealed a significant temperature spread among the overtone and multi-mode stars.  Our study provides new insights into the properties and evolution of RR Lyrae stars in globular clusters, highlighting the importance of considering overtone and multi-mode stars in our understanding of these objects. The results also have implications for the study of RR Lyrae stars in other globular clusters, and for our understanding of the complex interplay between stellar evolution, metallicity, and cluster properties.

This study investigates the covariant coarse-graining of inhomogeneous dust flow in the context of General Relativity. Inhomogeneous dust flows, which occur in astrophysical environments such as galaxy clusters and supernova remnants, pose significant challenges to traditional models of gravitational physics. The existing literature lacks a comprehensive framework for describing these flows in a covariant manner, particularly in the presence of non-trivial curvature and matter distributions.  The objective of this research is to develop a novel approach for covariant coarse-graining of inhomogeneous dust flows, enabling the accurate description of their dynamics and evolution. We employ a combination of numerical relativity techniques and coarse-graining methods, leveraging the flexibility of General Relativity to capture the complexities of inhomogeneous dust flows. Our approach involves the use of a novel, adaptive mesh refinement scheme, which allows for the efficient resolution of high-frequency modes and the accurate capture of low-frequency modes.  Our key findings indicate that the proposed approach is capable of accurately reproducing the dynamics of inhomogeneous dust flows in the presence of non-trivial curvature and matter distributions. We demonstrate the robustness of our results through a series of numerical tests, which reveal excellent agreement with existing simulations and theoretical predictions. The implications of our findings are significant, as they provide a new framework for understanding the behavior of inhomogeneous dust flows in a wide range of astrophysical contexts. Our results have the potential to inform future research in gravitational physics, cosmology, and the study of high-energy astrophysical phenomena.

Binary matroids have been extensively studied in combinatorial mathematics due to their significance in various applications. However, their restrictive binary nature limits their applicability in certain contexts. To expand the scope of matroid theory, the concept of powerful sets was introduced as a generalisation of binary matroids.   This paper aims to explore the fundamental properties, existence conditions, and applications of powerful sets as a generalisation of binary matroids.   We begin by introducing the definition of powerful sets and providing examples. We then investigate their relationship with binary matroids, focusing on their dependence, independence, and matroid intersection properties. Further, we discuss the existence conditions of powerful sets in different matroid structures, such as linearly dependent and linearly independent matroids. Lastly, we explore applications of powerful sets in network design problems.  Key findings Our research reveals that powerful sets have a richer structure than binary matroids, allowing for more complex dependencies and interactions. We show that powerful sets exhibit unique properties, such as having a basis that is linearly dependent in certain cases. Additionally, we demonstrate that powerful sets can be used to model and optimize various network design problems.   Powerful sets provide a valuable generalisation of binary matroids, expanding the applicability of matroid theory to more complex scenarios. By investigating their fundamental properties and exploring their potential applications, we contribute to a deeper understanding of this emerging area in combinatorial mathematics.

The inner accretion flow around supermassive black holes (SMBHs) plays a critical role in understanding their growth and the dynamics of surrounding matter. This study investigates the nature of the accretion flow in NGC 2617, a well-observed active galaxy hosting a SMBH. The primary objective was to directly probe the physical properties and behavior of the accretion flow using high-resolution spectroscopic observations from the Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based observatories during different states of activity. Employing a multi-wavelength approach, we analyzed the spectral signatures of emitted radiation, focusing on key emission lines that provide insight into the temperature, density, and kinematic properties of the innermost regions of the accretion disk. Our data revealed significant variability in the characteristics of the accretion flow, indicating transitions between different accretion states. Key findings illustrate that during heightened accretion phases, the inner disk becomes optically thick, while in quiescent phases, a transition to an optically thin state occurs. These results enhance our understanding of the accretion mechanisms at play and suggest that the accretion flow in NGC 2617 is influenced by both jet activity and disk instabilities. Ultimately, this research provides valuable insights into the dynamical processes surrounding SMBHs and their impact on galaxy evolution, underscoring the importance of observational studies in elucidating the complex behavior of accretion flows in active galactic nuclei.

Self-calibration is an essential process for robots to maintain their structural accuracy and enable reliable performance in various tasks. This study explores the self-calibration approach using multiple kinematic chains on the iCub humanoid robot through simulation. The background section discusses the challenges of self-calibration in robots and the benefits of using multiple kinematic chains. The objective of this research is to evaluate the effectiveness of this approach through computational simulations.  The methodology section outlines the simulation setup, including the iCub robot model, kinematic chains configuration, and the algorithms employed for calibration. The experimental part of this study involves applying various external perturbations to the iCub robot and recording the corresponding joint angles and end-effector positions. Then, by utilizing these data, the algorithms are executed to calculate the error matrices, which are subsequently used to find the calibration parameters.  The key findings section discusses the results of the simulation experiments, revealing the ability of multiple kinematic chains to accurately self-calibrate the iCub humanoid robot under external disturbances. This approach demonstrates significant improvement in the convergence rate and robustness when compared to traditional self-calibration methods. The study's conclusion highlights the implications of these findings in the realm of robotics, and the potential for this method to be implemented in real-world applications for enhancing robot precision and adaptability.

In this study, we explore algorithms for graph-constrained coalition formation in real-world scenarios. The problem at hand involves forming stable coalitions among rational agents while considering both the agents' preferences and the underlying graph structure that restricts allowable coalitions. Our aim is to develop efficient algorithms that can navigate these complexities to facilitate coalition formation in practical settings.   Through our research, we have achieved promising results in finding feasible coalition structures that satisfy all agents involved, taking into account the connectivity and compatibility constraints imposed by the underlying graph. To solve this problem, we propose a novel methodology that integrates graph theory principles with coalition formation algorithms. This approach enables us to identify stable coalitions that are not only individually rational but also cohesive within the given graph structure.  Our findings indicate that our algorithms effectively handle the challenges posed by graph constraints in coalition formation, resulting in coalitions that are both desirable for the agents and structurally sound within the graph. By combining theoretical insights with practical applications, we demonstrate the potential of our approach to address real-world coalition formation problems efficiently and effectively.

Analyzing the evolution of the hot flow of MAXI J1543-564, this research aims to investigate the behavior of this black hole X-ray binary. The objective is to understand how the hot flow in this system evolves over time and its impact on the overall accretion process. Utilizing observational data from MAXI and other telescopes, combined with theoretical models, the methodology involves tracking changes in the hot flow properties such as temperature, luminosity, and spectral characteristics. Key findings indicate variations in the hot flow properties over different phases of the outburst, with notable transitions in accretion modes. Furthermore, correlations between the hot flow evolution and the emergence of jet activity are explored. In conclusion, this study provides insights into the complex dynamics of the hot flow in MAXI J1543-564 and its role in the accretion processes of black hole X-ray binaries, contributing to the broader understanding of accretion-driven astrophysical phenomena.

This research investigates the modeling of X-ray light curves from the binary system Cygnus X-3, focusing on the potential influence of its relativistic jet. Historical data from X-ray observations, particularly those involving high-energy emission lines, are analyzed to understand the variability patterns. Employing advanced statistical techniques and numerical simulations, the study aims to elucidate the relationship between the jet dynamics and the observed X-ray flux variations. Key findings indicate that the jet can significantly modulate the X-ray emission, particularly during outburst phases when the jet's interaction with the accretion disk becomes more pronounced. The model suggests that the jet not only contributes to the variability but also affects the spectral properties, offering insights into the complex interplay between the central source and the surrounding environment. The conclusions emphasize the importance of considering jet effects in future models of Cygnus X-3 to achieve a more comprehensive understanding of this unique X-ray source.

This work reviews the state-of-the-art in Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) systems, emphasizing their significance in enhancing wireless communication performance through increased degrees of freedom. The study identifies the fundamental principles that underpin MIMO technology, including spatial multiplexing, diversity techniques, and beamforming. It analyzes various MIMO configurations such as single-user MIMO (SU-MIMO), multi-user MIMO (MU-MIMO), and massive MIMO, detailing their applications across different wireless standards like IEEE 802.11, LTE, and 5G. The research also examines recent advancements, including channel estimation methods, interference mitigation strategies, and novel coding schemes. Problematically, the increasing complexity of MIMO systems poses challenges in terms of computational efficiency, hardware requirements, and user experience. This work proposes potential solutions and future directions, focusing on energy-efficient designs, adaptive beamforming, and the integration of machine learning for dynamic channel adaptation. Key methodologies include theoretical analysis, simulation studies, and experimental validation using real-world datasets. The insights gained from this comprehensive review will guide researchers and practitioners in optimizing MIMO systems for future wireless networks.

In this study, we conduct an extensive characterization and selection process for silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) to be implemented in the photon detection system of the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) far detector. SiPMs are critical components in neutrino detection due to their high sensitivity and precision in low-light environments. Our primary objective is to identify SiPM models that offer optimal performance and reliability under the operational conditions anticipated in the DUNE setting, including high radiation environments and extremely low temperatures. We employ a rigorous methodology, involving both laboratory-based measurements and extensive simulation studies, to evaluate the performance characteristics of potential SiPM candidates. Key parameters assessed include photodetection efficiency, dark count rate, cross-talk probability, gain, and linearity. Our results indicate that certain SiPM configurations exhibit superior performance in maintaining high photodetection efficiency while minimizing noise and non-linearity issues, even in extreme conditions. We propose a selection criterion that integrates these performance metrics, which enables us to prioritize SiPM models that align best with DUNE's stringent requirements. Furthermore, our findings contribute to optimizing the overall sensitivity and accuracy of the DUNE far detector's photon detection system, thereby enhancing the experiment’s capability to study neutrino interactions. This research lays a foundational basis for the implementation of robust and efficient SiPM arrays in future neutrino detection systems, promoting advancements in neutrino physics research.

This study investigates the limitations of biometric-based mobile authentication and presents a secure alternative a multi-factor authentication system integrating One-Time Passwords (OTP) and Sensory Authentication (SA). The background section discusses the growing use of mobile devices for various transactions, making security a primary concern. Biometric authentication, despite its advantages, is susceptible to hacking, false acceptances, and privacy concerns.  The objective of this study is to provide an effective and secure mobile authentication solution, reducing reliance on biometric data while preserving user experience. The proposed methodology involves conducting a thorough literature review on mobile authentication methods, focusing on biometric-based and multi-factor approaches. The proposed system includes SMS OTP, which is relatively easy to implement and use, and SA, which incorporates touch, proximity, and face recognition to add an extra layer of security.  Key findings reveal that the proposed multi-factor authentication system significantly enhances the security of mobile transactions while maintaining user convenience. OTP provides an additional barrier against unauthorized access, and SA reduces false acceptances and potential privacy issues associated with biometric data. A simulation experiment shows a substantial decrease in the number of successful attacks compared to biometric-based authentication.  In conclusion, this study introduces a promising mobile authentication alternative to biometrics a multi-factor authentication system combining OTP and SA. This system ensures increased security through an added layer of authentication while maintaining a familiar and user-friendly experience.

This study explores the transition from localized to delocalized electronic states in materials under the influence of both local magnetic impurities (Kondo effect) and thermal fluctuations (Anderson disorder). The objective is to understand the interplay between these two mechanisms and their impact on the electronic properties of materials at the nanoscale. Employing density functional theory calculations and Monte Carlo simulations, we investigate various systems with varying levels of disorder and impurity concentration. Key findings indicate that the critical temperature for the onset of Anderson localization decreases as the strength of local magnetic impurities increases, leading to a broader range of Kondo temperatures. The results also suggest that the crossover from localized to delocalized states occurs at lower temperatures when impurities are more prevalent, highlighting the complex interdependence of local magnetic interactions and thermal effects. The conclusion underscores the importance of understanding these transitions in materials science and condensed matter physics, providing insights into the development of novel electronic devices and materials with tailored functionalities.

This study investigates the capability of single-reference coupled cluster (SRC) theory in describing static correlation within molecular systems. Our research employs SRC theory as a benchmark against more traditional methods such as complete active space self-consistent field (CASSCF) and multi-reference configuration interaction (MRCI). Theoretical predictions are compared with experimental data where available to assess the accuracy of SRC theory. We explore various levels of theory including single excitations, double excitations, and higher-order corrections to identify which components of static correlation are most accurately captured by SRC. Key methodologies involve optimizing the energy functional, incorporating appropriate basis sets, and employing efficient computational algorithms. Results indicate that while SRC theory can capture significant aspects of static correlation, particularly for small molecules, it struggles with larger systems and those involving complex electronic structures. This work highlights the strengths and limitations of SRC theory in the context of static correlation and provides insights into its potential applications and future developments.

This research paper delves into the realm of Smale's 7th problem, a longstanding challenge in the field of chaos theory and dynamical systems. The problem, proposed by Stephen Smale in 1967, revolves around the existence of a diffeomorphism of the 7-dimensional sphere that is not homotopic to the identity map. The "magic" numbers associated with this problem have been a subject of intense investigation, as they hold the key to resolving the problem.  The objective of this study is to explore the properties of the magic numbers and their relationship to the topology of the 7-dimensional sphere. A comprehensive analysis of the existing literature on Smale's 7th problem is conducted, with a focus on the role of magic numbers in the problem's resolution. The methodology employed in this study involves a combination of mathematical modeling, numerical simulations, and topological analysis.  Key findings of this research include the identification of a new set of magic numbers that satisfy the conditions of Smale's 7th problem. These numbers are found to be intimately connected with the topology of the 7-dimensional sphere, and their properties are used to construct a new diffeomorphism that is not homotopic to the identity map. The implications of these findings are significant, as they provide new insights into the nature of chaos and complexity in dynamical systems.  The study concludes that the magic numbers play a crucial role in the resolution of Smale's 7th problem, and their properties are essential for understanding the topology of the 7-dimensional sphere. The research contributes to the ongoing debate in the field of chaos theory and dynamical systems, and its findings have the potential to shed new light on the fundamental laws governing the behavior of complex systems.

In this study, we compare grid-based and Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations to investigate binary mass-transfer and merger processes. We focus on simulating the accretion phase during which one star transfers material to another through Roche lobe overflow, leading to mergers when sufficient mass transfer occurs. The grid-based simulations utilize finite volume methods to discretize the computational domain, while SPH employs a particle-based approach where fluid elements are represented as discrete particles. Our key findings indicate that both methods capture the essential physics of mass transfer and merger dynamics effectively, but they differ in their treatment of boundary conditions and numerical viscosity. SPH is advantageous in capturing complex flows and shocks more naturally, whereas grid-based methods offer better control over numerical diffusion and can handle large dynamic ranges more efficiently. We also find that the choice between these two methods significantly impacts the accuracy and stability of the simulation outcomes. The methodologies employed include detailed comparisons of density profiles, velocity fields, and merger timescales, validating the robustness of each approach under various initial conditions. This comparison highlights the strengths and limitations of each technique, providing insights for future research directions and applications in astrophysical modeling.

We investigate the feasibility of utilizing transceivers in motion to enable person localization within buildings, overcoming the traditional limitations of traditional localization methods. Our approach leverages the principles of radio frequency (RF) signal propagation to derive a novel localization algorithm. We design and implement a system consisting of a transmitter and multiple receivers, which are dynamically moved within the building to capture RF signals from a person in motion. By analyzing the received signal strength and time-of-arrival, we develop a machine learning-based model to predict the person's location.  Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed system, achieving an average localization accuracy of 95.6% with a median error of 2.5 meters. We observe that the system's performance is significantly enhanced when the transceivers are moved in synchronization with the person's movement, resulting in a reduction of localization errors by 30.4%. Our results also reveal that the system can localize individuals in complex environments with multiple floors and obstacles, showcasing its potential for real-world applications.  The key to our success lies in the integration of advanced signal processing techniques, including time-frequency analysis and machine learning algorithms. By harnessing the unique characteristics of RF signals, we are able to develop a robust and accurate localization system that can adapt to various scenarios. Our findings have significant implications for various fields, including indoor navigation, surveillance, and emergency response.

This study explores realistic compactification within spatially flat vacuum cosmological models in cubic Lovelock gravity, focusing on low-dimensional cases. The primary objective is to investigate how compactification can lead to viable cosmological solutions that resemble our observed universe, particularly in scenarios where higher-order curvature terms dominate. The research employs analytical and numerical methods to explore the dynamics of spacetime, emphasizing the interplay between gravitational theories and compactified dimensions. Key findings indicate that under certain conditions, compactification can result in effective four-dimensional gravity with properties similar to those of Einstein's theory, including a late-time acceleration consistent with observations. The study highlights the importance of Lovelock gravity in providing a framework for understanding compactified dimensions and their impact on cosmological evolution. The conclusion underscores the potential of these models to offer insights into the nature of dark energy and the structure of spacetime, while also suggesting avenues for further theoretical exploration and experimental verification.

This study investigates monotone switching networks (MSNs) for directed connectivity and demonstrates that they are strictly more powerful than certain-knowledge switching networks (CKSNs). The research begins by defining the computational capabilities of both MSNs and CKSNs. Through theoretical analysis and simulation experiments, we establish that MSNs can compute a broader class of functions compared to CKSNs, even when considering the same number of switches and inputs. Key methodologies include constructing benchmark problems and applying different switching network configurations to these problems. The findings reveal that while both types of networks have their unique strengths, MSNs excel in scenarios requiring strict monotonicity and directionality in signal flow. This insight contributes to a deeper understanding of the comparative power and applicability of different switching network architectures in computational tasks.

The study investigates the interconnections between integral probability metrics, \(\phi\)-divergences, and binary classification problems, aiming to enhance the understanding and application of these mathematical tools in statistical learning models. Integral probability metrics (IPMs) and \(\phi\)-divergences serve as pivotal instruments for measuring discrepancies between probability distributions, offering utility in various fields, particularly machine learning. The objective of this research is to elucidate the relationships among these metrics and their implications for binary classification tasks. To achieve this, we examine a unified theoretical framework comprising both IPMs and \(\phi\)-divergences, identifying conditions under which they can be utilized interchangeably or complementarily in model assessment and selection. Using rigorous mathematical analysis, we derive bounds and inequalities that relate different IPMs and \(\phi\)-divergences, thereby facilitating their application in real-world binary classification scenarios. The key findings reveal that certain IPMs can effectively approximate \(\phi\)-divergences under specific conditions, and vice versa, providing a deeper grasp of the metrics' roles in classification accuracy. Additionally, the research identifies scenarios where these relationships yield practical benefits, such as improved model generalization and robustness. In conclusion, the unified perspective on IPMs and \(\phi\)-divergences enhances the strategic deployment of these metrics in binary classification, offering insights into selecting the appropriate metric for specific data characteristics and classification goals. This study contributes to the optimization of model evaluation techniques, paving the way for more precise and effective applications in machine learning.

Among the Milky Way satellites discovered in the past three years, Triangulum
II has presented the most difficulty in revealing its dynamical status. Kirby
et al. (2015a) identified it as the most dark matter-dominated galaxy known,
with a mass-to-light ratio within the half-light radius of 3600 +3500 -2100
M_sun/L_sun. On the other hand, Martin et al. (2016) measured an outer velocity
dispersion that is 3.5 +/- 2.1 times larger than the central velocity
dispersion, suggesting that the system might not be in equilibrium. From new
multi-epoch Keck/DEIMOS measurements of 13 member stars in Triangulum II, we
constrain the velocity dispersion to be sigma_v < 3.4 km/s (90% C.L.). Our
previous measurement of sigma_v, based on six stars, was inflated by the
presence of a binary star with variable radial velocity. We find no evidence
that the velocity dispersion increases with radius. The stars display a wide
range of metallicities, indicating that Triangulum II retained supernova ejecta
and therefore possesses or once possessed a massive dark matter halo. However,
the detection of a metallicity dispersion hinges on the membership of the two
most metal-rich stars. The stellar mass is lower than galaxies of similar mean
stellar metallicity, which might indicate that Triangulum II is either a star
cluster or a tidally stripped dwarf galaxy. Detailed abundances of one star
show heavily depressed neutron-capture abundances, similar to stars in most
other ultra-faint dwarf galaxies but unlike stars in globular clusters.

The following two decision problems capture the complexity of comparing
integers or rationals that are succinctly represented in
product-of-exponentials notation, or equivalently, via arithmetic circuits
using only multiplication and division gates, and integer inputs:
  Input instance: four lists of positive integers: a_1, ...., a_n ; b_1,....,
b_n ; c_1,....,c_m ; d_1, ...., d_m ; where each of the integers is represented
in binary.
  Problem 1 (equality testing): Decide whether a_1^{b_1} a_2^{b_2} ....
a_n^{b_n} = c_1^{d_1} c_2^{d_2} .... c_m^{d_m} .
  Problem 2 (inequality testing): Decide whether a_1^{b_1} a_2^{b_2} ...
a_n^{b_n} >= c_1^{d_1} c_2^{d_2} .... c_m^{d_m} .
  Problem 1 is easily decidable in polynomial time using a simple iterative
algorithm. Problem 2 is much harder. We observe that the complexity of Problem
2 is intimately connected to deep conjectures and results in number theory. In
particular, if a refined form of the ABC conjecture formulated by Baker in 1998
holds, or if the older Lang-Waldschmidt conjecture (formulated in 1978) on
linear forms in logarithms holds, then Problem 2 is decidable in P-time (in the
standard Turing model of computation). Moreover, it follows from the best
available quantitative bounds on linear forms in logarithms, e.g., by Baker and
W\"{u}stholz (1993) or Matveev (2000), that if m and n are fixed universal
constants then Problem 2 is decidable in P-time (without relying on any
conjectures). This latter fact was observed earlier by Shub (1993).
  We describe one application: P-time maximum probability parsing for arbitrary
stochastic context-free grammars (where \epsilon-rules are allowed).

We show the combined spectral analysis of \emph{Chandra} high energy
transmission grating (HETG) and \emph{XMM-Newton} reflection grating
spectrometer (RGS) observations of the broad-line radio galaxy 3C 111. The
source is known to show excess neutral absorption with respect to the one
estimated from 21 cm radio surveys of atomic H I in the Galaxy. However,
previous works were not able to constrain the origin of such absorber as local
to our Milky Way or intrinsic to the source ($z = 0.0485$). The high
signal-to-noise grating spectra allow us to constrain the excess absorption as
due to intervening gas in the Milky Way, and we estimate a time averaged total
column density of $N_H = (7.4\pm0.1)\times 10^{21}$ cm$^{-2}$, a factor of two
higher than the tabulated H I value. We recommend to use the total average
Galactic column density here estimated when studying 3C 111. The origin of the
extra Galactic absorption of $N_H = 4.4\times 10^{21}$ cm$^{-2}$ is likely due
to molecular gas associated with the Taurus molecular cloud complex toward 3C
111, which is our nearest star-forming region. We also detect a weak
(EW$=$$16\pm10$ eV) and narrow (FWMH$<$5,500 km s$^{-1}$, consistent with
optical H$\alpha$) Fe K$\alpha$ emission line at E$=$6.4 keV likely from the
torus in the central regions of 3C 111, and we place an upper limit on the
column density of a possible intrinsic warm absorber of
$N_H$$<$$2.5\times10^{20}$ cm$^{-2}$. These complexities make 3C 111 a very
promising object for studying both the intrinsic properties of this active
radio galaxy and the Galactic interstellar medium if used as a background
source.

We present a supersymmetric SO(10) grand unified theory (GUT) of flavor based
on an $S_4$ family symmetry. It makes use of our recent proposal to use SO(10)
with type II seesaw mechanism for neutrino masses combined with a simple ansatz
that the dominant Yukawa matrix (the {\bf 10}-Higgs coupling to matter) has
rank one. In this paper, we show how the rank one model can arise within some
plausible assumptions as an effective field theory from vectorlike {\bf 16}
dimensional matter fields with masses above the GUT scale. In order to obtain
the desired fermion flavor texture we use $S_4$ flavon multiplets which acquire
vevs in the ground state of the theory. By supplementing the $S_4$ theory with
an additional discrete symmetry, we find that the flavon vacuum field
alignments take a discrete set of values provided some of the higher
dimensional couplings are small. Choosing a particular set of these vacuum
alignments appears to lead to an unified understanding of observed quark-lepton
flavor:
  (i) the lepton mixing matrix that is dominantly tri-bi-maximal with small
corrections related to quark mixings; (ii) quark lepton mass relations at GUT
scale: $m_b\simeq m_{\tau}$ and $m_\mu\simeq 3 m_s$ and (iii) the solar to
atmospheric neutrino mass ratio $m_\odot/m_{\rm atm}\simeq \theta_{\rm
Cabibbo}$ in agreement with observations. The model predicts the neutrino
mixing parameter, $U_{e3} \simeq \theta_{\rm Cabibbo}/(3\sqrt2) \sim 0.05$,
which should be observable in planned long baseline experiments.

The detection by Rest et al. (2012) of light echoes from $\eta$ Carinae has
provided important new observational constraints on the nature of its 1840's
era giant eruption. Spectra of the echoes suggest a relatively cool spectral
temperature of about 5500K, lower than the lower limit of about 7000K suggested
in the optically thick wind outflow analysis of Davidson (1987). This has lead
to a debate about the viability of this steady wind model relative to
alternative, explosive scenarios. Here we present an updated analysis of the
wind outflow model using newer low-temperature opacity tabulations and
accounting for the stronger mass loss implied by the $>$10 Msun mass now
inferred for the Homunculus. A major conclusion is that, because of the sharp
drop in opacity due to free electron recombination for $T<$6500K, a low
temperature of about 5000K is compatible with, and indeed expected from, a wind
with the extreme mass loss inferred for the eruption. Within a spherical gray
model in radiative equilibrium, we derive spectral energy distributions for
various assumptions for the opacity variation of the wind, providing a basis
for comparisons with observed light echo spectra. The scaling results here are
also potentially relevant for other highly optically thick outflows, including
those from classical novae, giant eruptions of LBVs and SN Type IIn precursors.
A broader issue therefore remains whether the complex, variable features
observed from such eruptions are better understood in terms of a steady or
explosive paradigm, or perhaps a balance of these idealizations.

This paper concerns with the group zero-norm regularized least squares
estimator which, in terms of the variational characterization of the zero-norm,
can be obtained from a mathematical program with equilibrium constraints
(MPEC). By developing the global exact penalty for the MPEC, this estimator is
shown to arise from an exact penalization problem that not only has a favorable
bilinear structure but also implies a recipe to deliver equivalent DC
estimators such as the SCAD and MCP estimators. We propose a multi-stage convex
relaxation approach (GEP-MSCRA) for computing this estimator, and under a
restricted strong convexity assumption on the design matrix, establish its
theoretical guarantees which include the decreasing of the error bounds for the
iterates to the true coefficient vector and the coincidence of the iterates
after finite steps with the oracle estimator. Finally, we implement the
GEP-MSCRA with the subproblems solved by a semismooth Newton augmented
Lagrangian method (ALM) and compare its performance with that of SLEP and
MALSAR, the solvers for the weighted $\ell_{2,1}$-norm regularized estimator,
on synthetic group sparse regression problems and real multi-task learning
problems. Numerical comparison indicates that the GEP-MSCRA has significant
advantage in reducing error and achieving better sparsity than the SLEP and the
MALSAR do.

We present new brightness and magnetic images of the weak-line T Tauri star
V410 Tau, made using data from the NARVAL spectropolarimeter at Telescope
Bernard Lyot (TBL). The brightness image shows a large polar spot and
significant spot coverage at lower latitudes. The magnetic maps show a field
that is predominantly dipolar and non-axisymmetric with a strong azimuthal
component. The field is 50% poloidal and 50% toroidal, and there is very little
differential rotation apparent from the magnetic images.
  A photometric monitoring campaign on this star has previously revealed V-band
variability of up to 0.6 magnitudes but in 2009 the lightcurve is much flatter.
The Doppler image presented here is consistent with this low variability.
Calculating the flux predicted by the mapped spot distribution gives an
peak-to-peak variability of 0.04 magnitudes. The reduction in the amplitude of
the lightcurve, compared with previous observations, appears to be related to a
change in the distribution of the spots, rather than the number or area.
  This paper is the first from a Zeeman-Doppler imaging campaign being carried
out on V410 Tau between 2009-2012 at TBL. During this time it is expected that
the lightcurve will return to a high amplitude state, allowing us to ascertain
whether the photometric changes are accompanied by a change in the magnetic
field topology.

We consider a large-scale service system model motivated by the problem of
efficient placement of virtual machines to physical host machines in a network
cloud, so that the total number of occupied hosts is minimized. Customers of
different types arrive to a system with an infinite number of servers. A server
packing configuration is the vector $k = (k_i)$, where $k_i$ is the number of
type-$i$ customers that the server "contains". Packing constraints are
described by a fixed finite set of allowed configurations. Upon arrival, each
customer is placed into a server immediately, subject to the packing
constraints; the server can be idle or already serving other customers. After
service completion, each customer leaves its server and the system.
  It was shown recently that a simple real-time algorithm, called Greedy, is
asymptotically optimal in the sense of minimizing $\sum_k X_k^{1+\alpha}$ in
the stationary regime, as the customer arrival rates grow to infinity. (Here
\alpha >0, and $X_k$ denotes the number of servers with configuration $k$.) In
particular, when parameter \alpha is small, Greedy approximately solves the
problem of minimizing $\sum_k X_k$, the number of occupied hosts. In this paper
we introduce the algorithm called Greedy with sublinear Safety Stocks (GSS),
and show that it asymptotically solves the exact problem of minimizing $\sum_k
X_k$. An important feature of the algorithm is that sublinear safety stocks of
$X_k$ are created automatically - when and where necessary - without having to
determine a priori where they are required. Moreover, we also provide a tight
characterization of the rate of convergence to optimality under GSS. The GSS
algorithm is as simple as Greedy, and uses no more system state information
than Greedy does.

As a step toward analyzing second-harmonic generation (SHG) from crystalline
Si nanospheres in glass, we develop an anisotropic bond model (ABM) that
expresses SHG in terms of physically meaningful parameters and provides a
detailed understanding of the basic physics of SHG on the atomic scale.
Nonlinear-optical (NLO) responses are calculated classically via the four
fundamental steps of optics: evaluate the local field at a given bond site,
solve the force equation for the acceleration of the charge, calculate the
resulting radiation, then superpose the radiation from all charges. The ABM
goes beyond previous bond models by including the complete set of underlying
contributions: retardation (RD), spatial-dispersion (SD), and magnetic (MG)
effects, in addition to the anharmonic restoring force acting on the bond
charge. We apply the ABM to obtain analytic expressions for SHG from amorphous
materials under Gaussian-beam excitation. These materials represent an
interesting test case not only because they are ubiquitous but also because the
anharmonic-force contribution that dominates the SHG response of crystalline
materials and ordered interfaces vanishes by symmetry. Using the paraxial-ray
approximation, we reduce the results to the isotropic case in two limits, that
where the linear restoring force dominates (glasses), and that where it is
absent (metals). Both forward- and backscattering geometries are discussed.
Estimated signal strengths and conversion efficiencies for fused silica appear
to be in general agreement with data, where available. Predictions are made
that allow additional critical tests of these results.

We present a simple neural network model which combines a locally-connected
feedforward structure, as is traditionally used to model inter-neuron
connectivity, with a layer of undifferentiated connections which model the
diffuse projections from the human limbic system to the cortex. This new layer
makes it possible to model global effects such as salience, at the same time as
the local network processes task-specific or local information. This simple
combination network displays interactions between salience and regular
processing which correspond to known effects in the developing brain, such as
enhanced learning as a result of heightened affect.
  The cortex biases neuronal responses to affect both learning and memory,
through the use of diffuse projections from the limbic system to the cortex.
Standard ANNs do not model this non-local flow of information represented by
the ascending systems, which are a significant feature of the structure of the
brain, and although they do allow associational learning with multiple-trial,
they simply don't provide the capacity for one-time learning.
  In this research we model this effect using an artificial neural network
(ANN), creating a salience-affected neural network (SANN). We adapt an ANN to
embody the capacity to respond to an input salience signal and to produce a
reverse salience signal during testing.
  This research demonstrates that input combinations similar to the inputs in
the training data sets will produce similar reverse salience signals during
testing. Furthermore, this research has uncovered a novel method for training
ANNs with a single training iteration.

The visualization of any graph plays important role in various aspects, such
as graph drawing software. Complex systems (like large databases or networks)
that have a graph structure should be properly visualized in order to avoid
obfuscation. One way to provide an aesthetic improvement to a graph
visualization is to apply a force-directed drawing algorithm to it. This
method, that emerged in the 60's views graphs as spring systems that exert
forces (repulsive or attractive) to the nodes.
  A Lombardi drawing of a graph is a drawing where the edges are drawn as
circular arcs (straight edges are considered circular arcs of infinite radius)
with perfect angular resolution. This means, that consecutive edges around a
vertex are equally spaced around it. In other words, each angle between the
tangents of two consecutive edges is equal to $2\pi/d$ where d is the degree of
that specific vertex. The requirement of using circular edges in graphs when we
want to provide perfect angular resolution is necessary, since even cycle
graphs cannot be drawn with straight edges when perfect angular resolution is
needed.
  In this survey, we provide an algorithm that takes as input a random drawing
of a graph and provides its Lombardi drawing, giving a proper visualization of
the graph.

The scission kinetics of bottle-brush molecules in solution and on an
adhesive substrate is modeled by means of Molecular Dynamics simulation with
Langevin thermostat. Our macromolecules comprise a long flexible polymer
backbone with $L$ segments, consisting of breakable bonds, along with two side
chains of length $N$, tethered to each segment of the backbone. In agreement
with recent experiments and theoretical predictions, we find that bond cleavage
is significantly enhanced on a strongly attractive substrate even though the
chemical nature of the bonds remains thereby unchanged.
  We find that the mean bond life time $<\tau>$ decreases upon adsorption by
more than an order of magnitude even for brush molecules with comparatively
short side chains $N=1 \div 4$. The distribution of scission probability along
the bonds of the backbone is found to be rather sensitive regarding the
interplay between length and grafting density of side chains. The life time
$<\tau>$ declines with growing contour length $L$ as $<\tau>\propto L^{-0.17}$,
and with side chain length as $<\tau>\propto N^{-0.53}$. The probability
distribution of fragment lengths at different times agrees well with
experimental observations. The variation of the mean length $L(t)$ of the
fragments with elapsed time confirms the notion of the thermal degradation
process as a first order reaction.

In this paper we continue studying the decay of unstable FZZT branes
initiated in [1],[2]. The mass of tachyonic mode in this model can be chosen
arbitrarily small and we use it as a perturbative parameter. In [2] a
time-dependent boundary conformal field theory (BCFT) describing the decay
process was studied and it was shown that in a certain sense this BCFT
interpolates between two stationary BCFT's corresponding to the UV and IR fixed
points of the associated RG flow. In the present work we find in the leading
order vertex operators of the time-dependent BCFT. We identify the "in" and
"out" vertex operators assigned to the UV and IR fixed points and compute the
related Bogolyubov coefficients. We show that there is a codimension one
subspace of the out-going states for which pair creation amplitudes are
independent of the initial wave function of the tachyonic mode. We demonstrate
that such amplitudes can be computed within the framework of first quantized
open string theory via suitably defined string two-point functions. We also
evaluate a three point function which we interpret as an amplitude for string
triplet creation due to interaction. Some peculiarities of scattering
amplitudes in the presence of tachyonic modes in the far past are discussed.

A unitary coupled-channels model is presented for investigating the decays of
heavy mesons and excited meson states into three light pseudoscalar mesons. The
model accounts for the three-mesons final state interactions in the decay
processes, as required by both the three-body and two-body unitarity
conditions. In the absence of the Z-diagram mechanisms that are necessary
consequences of the three-body unitarity, our decay amplitudes are reduced to a
form similar to those used in the so-called isobar-model analysis. We apply our
coupled-channels model to the three-pions decays of a1(1260), pi2(1670),
pi2(2100), and D0 mesons, and show that the Z-diagram mechanisms can contribute
to the calculated Dalitz plot distributions by as much as 30% in magnitudes in
the regions where f0(600), rho(770), and f2(1270) dominate the distributions.
Also, by fitting to the same Dalitz plot distributions, we demonstrate that the
decay amplitudes obtained with the unitary model and the isobar model can be
rather different, particularly in the phase that plays a crucial role in
extracting the CKM CP-violating phase from the data of B meson decays. Our
results indicate that the commonly used isobar model analysis must be extended
to account for the final state interactions required by the three-body
unitarity to reanalyze the three-mesons decays of heavy mesons, thereby
exploring hybrid or exotic mesons, and signatures of physics beyond the
standard model.

Halal is a notion that applies to both objects and actions, and means
permissible according to Islamic law. It may be most often associated with food
and the rules of selecting, slaughtering, and cooking animals. In the
globalized world, halal can be found in street corners of New York and beauty
shops of Manila. In this study, we explore the cultural diversity of the
concept, as revealed through social media, and specifically the way it is
expressed by different populations around the world, and how it relates to
their perception of (i) religious and (ii) governmental authority, and (iii)
personal health. Here, we analyze two Instagram datasets, using Halal in Arabic
(325,665 posts) and in English (1,004,445 posts), which provide a global view
of major Muslim populations around the world. We find a great variety in the
use of halal within Arabic, English, and Indonesian-speaking populations, with
animal trade emphasized in first (making up 61% of the language's stream), food
in second (80%), and cosmetics and supplements in third (70%). The
commercialization of the term halal is a powerful signal of its detraction from
its traditional roots. We find a complex social engagement around posts
mentioning religious terms, such that when a food-related post is accompanied
by a religious term, it on average gets more likes in English and Indonesian,
but not in Arabic, indicating a potential shift out of its traditional moral
framing.

Rapid accretion of cold gas plays a crucial role in getting gas into
galaxies. It has been suggested that this accretion proceeds along narrow
streams that might also directly drive the turbulence in galactic gas,
dynamical disturbances, and bulge formation. In cosmological simulations,
however, it is impossible to isolate and hence disentangle the effect of
accretion from internal instabilities and mergers. Moreover, in most
cosmological simulations, the phase structure and turbulence in the ISM arising
from stellar feedback are treated in a sub-grid manner, so that feedback cannot
generate ISM turbulence. In this paper we therefore test the effects of cold
streams in extremely high-resolution simulations of otherwise isolated galaxy
disks using detailed models for star formation and feedback; we then include or
exclude mock cold flows falling onto the galaxies with accretion rates,
velocities and geometry set to maximize their effect on the disk. We find: (1)
Turbulent velocity dispersions in gas disks are identical with or without the
cold flow; the energy injected by the flow is dissipated where it meets the
disk. (2) In runs without stellar feedback, the presence of a cold flow has
essentially no effect on runaway local collapse, resulting in star formation
rates (SFRs) that are far too large. (3) Disks in runs with feedback and cold
flows have higher SFRs, but only insofar as they have more gas. (4) Because
flows are extended relative to the disk, they do not trigger strong resonant
responses and so induce weak morphological perturbation (bulge formation via
instabilities is not accelerated). (5) However, flows can thicken the disk by
direct contribution of out-of-plane streams. We conclude that while inflows are
critical over cosmological timescales to determine the supply and angular
momentum of gas disks, they have weak instantaneous dynamical effects on
galaxies.

Based on our previous work (Vidotto et al. 2009a), we investigate the effects
on the wind and magnetospheric structures of weak-lined T Tauri stars due to a
misalignment between the axis of rotation of the star and its magnetic dipole
moment vector. In such configuration, the system loses the axisymmetry
presented in the aligned case, requiring a fully 3D approach. We perform 3D
numerical MHD simulations of stellar winds and study the effects caused by
different model parameters. The system reaches a periodic behavior with the
